summary: The row that grades the `MAX_MATCH_INPUT` input clamp asserts `Date.now() - started < 100`, but is run at input lengths where an unclamped match never returns. Remove the clamp and the case does not go red — it wedges the vitest worker in synchronous backtracking that no test timeout can preempt.
failure: Mutate `Allowlist.has` (allowlist.ts:126) `if (topic.length > MAX_MATCH_INPUT) return false;` -> `if (false) return false;`. Row `four unbounded quantifiers @ 5000 (no match)` then evaluates `/^(?:.*.*.*.*x)$/.test('a'.repeat(4999)+'!')`. Measured on this machine: 512 chars = 2.06s, 256 = 152ms, growth ~n^3 (compositions of n into 4 parts), so 5000 chars is ~30 minutes of uninterruptible sync work. Observed: `npx vitest run packages/bridge-core/src/allowlist.test.ts` hit a 200s wall timeout with no result, and the earlier full-package run sat >15 minutes on this one mutation. CI sees a hung job, not a named failing test.
remediation: Grade the clamp structurally instead of by wall clock: wrap each compiled pattern in a counting proxy (or spy on `RegExp.prototype.test`) and assert that a topic longer than `MAX_MATCH_INPUT` causes ZERO pattern evaluations, then keep only non-catastrophic patterns at the 256/5000 lengths for the verdict rows. If the timing assertion is kept, restrict `.*.*.*.*x` to lengths <= 256, where the unclamped case already exceeds the 100ms budget (measured 152ms) and still terminates.
testUpgrade: Parameterize the CLASS: any assertion that a bound holds by timing a regex/glob against caller-supplied input must be paired with a structural observation (call count, or a matcher wrapped to throw once invoked past the bound) so removing the bound produces a red row, not a hang. Add a row asserting `has(overLongTopic)` evaluates no pattern at all; apply the same shape to `identity-filter.test.ts`'s `performance.now() < 100` rows.

remediationCheck.reliesOn: `Allowlist.has`'s ordering — the clamp sits ahead of `this.patternRegexes.some((re) => re.test(topic))`, so counting `re.test` invocations is a faithful observation of the clamp; and `MATCH_ROWS`'s existing derived verdict `len <= MAX_MATCH_INPUT`.
remediationCheck.newlyAccepts: none — the verdict column is unchanged.
remediationCheck.newlyRejects: a `has()` implementation that clamps by returning false only AFTER evaluating the patterns (same answer, unbounded work) — today's timing row would pass that at short lengths.
remediationCheck.testsThatWouldFail: none found. I ran allowlist.test.ts, regex-safety.test.ts, stated-bounds.test.ts and readme-truth.test.ts against the unmutated tree; the `MAX_MATCH_INPUT` bound is also graded in stated-bounds.test.ts (BOUNDS row) and readme-truth.test.ts, both of which use short inputs and are unaffected by dropping the 5000-length row for one pattern.
remediationCheck.hidesOrFixes: If the timing assertion is left and only the length capped, a clamp regression is caught at 256 with a real red row instead of a hang — the bug is still caught. If neither is done, the guard remains one that can only hang.

summary: `CORE_VERSION` is the `serverInfo.version` every MCP client sees on `initialize`, and nothing anywhere asserts it equals the package manifest. Its own doc explains that a hardcoded constant would drift — yet a hardcoded constant keeps the suite green.
failure: Replace the whole module body with `export const CORE_VERSION: string = '9.9.9-mutant';` and `npx vitest run packages/bridge-core` reports `Test Files 54 passed / Tests 3283 passed`. Every stdio and remote client then advertises 9.9.9-mutant with no test objecting. The path `new URL('../package.json', import.meta.url)` is correct today only because `rootDir: src`/`outDir: dist` makes the src and dist depths coincide; a tsconfig change emitting `dist/src/version.js` breaks the package at IMPORT time (top-level readFileSync -> ENOENT) while the suite, which runs from `src/`, still resolves and stays green.

Grade the dist resolution too: assert `new URL('../package.json', pathToFileURL(join(dir,'dist','version.js')))` names the package manifest for every public workspace that reads its version this way (packaging.test.ts already walks that set).
testUpgrade: Parameterize over the CLASS `a value derived from package.json at runtime`: for every public workspace, (a) the derived constant equals the manifest, and (b) the relative path it derives it through resolves from the EMITTED location, not only from `src/`. That catches the next `bin` or transport that computes a version from `import.meta.url` — `cli/backend-cli.ts`'s `versionOf(moduleUrl)` has the identical shape and is only graded by conformance spawning built bins.

remediationCheck.reliesOn: `packaging.test.ts`'s `publicWorkspaces()` (read out of `scripts/lib/workspaces.mjs`) for the workspace set, and `isEmitted(tsconfig, file)` for the emit-path derivation — both already exist and already floor themselves.
remediationCheck.newlyRejects: a version.ts whose constant is a literal, and a tsconfig whose rootDir change moves the emitted file relative to package.json — both accepted today.
remediationCheck.testsThatWouldFail: none found. The new assertion pins CORE_VERSION to `0.1.0` transitively via the manifest, and the release stamps package.json, so `scripts/stamp-version.mjs` keeps it true. I checked stated-bounds.test.ts's capacity walk: it takes only NUMBER exports, so a string constant adds no row there.

failure: `grep -n 'parley-\(slack\|zulip\|sqlite\|matrix\|redis\)' packages/bridge-core/src` returns backend-cli.ts:9-10 (a comment: "`parley-slack --help` died on a missing config file and `parley-zulip --confg prod.yaml` started a bridge against the default deployment") and config-diagnostics.ts:42 (a shipped runtime string suggesting `'parley-sqlite, parley-matrix, parley-redis, …'`). `PLUGIN_REFERENCE = /\bbridge-(?:sqlite|redis|…)\b/` misses all of them, so the rule whose own message reads "core explains itself without naming a backend PACKAGE" grades nothing here. summary: The ReDoS screen is calibrated per SOURCE ("single-digit milliseconds") and the collection is capped at 64, but nothing bounds the product. A config `parseConfig` fully accepts makes every allowlist miss cost 100ms of synchronous event-loop time.
failure: `post_topics` = 64 distinct sources of the form `[a-z]{0,64}[a-z]{0,64}[a-z]{0,64}[a-z]{0,64}z<i>` — each screens safe (budget 16^4 = 65536 = exactly MAX_AMBIGUITY) and `parseConfig` accepts all 64. Measured in this tree: `allowlistFor(cfg).has('a'.repeat(64))` returns false after 100.0ms of blocking work. Every `parley_post` / `parley_reply` / `parley_fetch_recent` / topic-scoped `parley_list_users` on a non-allowlisted topic pays it, so ~10 tool calls/sec from one authenticated client (or one prompt-injected agent loop) pins the single-threaded server, stalling every other client, the presence heartbeat and the long-poll.
remediation: Bound the COLLECTION, not only each member: have `regex-safety` expose the numeric budget it already computes (e.g. `redosBudget(src): number` returning `budget`, with `isRedosSafeSource` = `redosBudget(src) <= MAX_AMBIGUITY`), and have the `Allowlist` constructor and the `post_topics` superRefine reject when the SUM over sources exceeds a stated collection bound. Alternatively lower `MAX_POST_TOPICS`, but that trades a stated operator capacity for the same effect.
testUpgrade: Add an aggregate-cost row to the CLASS of screened collections, parameterized over every site that holds one (`Allowlist.postPatterns`, `presence-reach`'s peer `postTopics`): fill the collection to its cap with maximum-budget sources and assert one miss stays under a stated aggregate budget. Widen `regex-safety.test.ts`'s existing 'a screened collection is bounded in aggregate' describe from a membership/cap assertion to a measured aggregate one, so filling the cap with worst-case members is what the row exercises.

remediationCheck.reliesOn: `isRedosSafeSource`'s internal `budget` accumulator and `charge()` clamp at `Number.MAX_SAFE_INTEGER`; the branch depended on is the final `return budget <= MAX_AMBIGUITY`, which is exactly the number to surface.
remediationCheck.newlyRejects: a config whose 64 `post_topics` are each individually safe but jointly expensive — e.g. the 64-pattern set above. Legitimate broad sets (`ctx-.*` x64, budget 16 each) stay well inside any sane collection bound.
remediationCheck.testsThatWouldFail: `stated-bounds.test.ts > has a row for every numeric capacity anything under src/ exports` FAILS the moment a new numeric export (a collection bound) is added, until a CAPACITIES row with `expected`/`accepts`/`refusesPast` is written — I read `declaredCapacities()`, it walks `import.meta.glob('./**/*.ts')` and requires an exact set match. `regex-screen-parity.test.ts > pins the corpus membership` is unaffected (single-source rows). No existing SAFE_PATTERNS row uses 64 patterns at once.
remediationCheck.hidesOrFixes: If only `MAX_POST_TOPICS` is lowered, the per-call cost drops proportionally but the class remains: `presence-reach` holds a screened collection of ATTACKER-supplied sources under `MAX_RECORD_TOPICS` and has the same unbounded product. The aggregate budget is what closes both.

summary: `assertKnownConfigKeys` iterates `declared.nested` and `continue`s when the named key is absent from the config, so a `nested` key that is not one of `declared.keys` — a plugin-author typo — silently disables that whole nested check with no error, which is the opposite of this function's stated fail-fast contract.
failure: Given `{ keys: ['tls', …], nested: { tsl: ['ca_file','cert_file','key_file'] } }` (one transposition), `assertKnownConfigKeys('nats', { tls: { ca_flie: '/etc/ca.pem' } }, DECLARED)` returns normally: the top loop finds `tls` in `keys` and passes it; the nested loop reads `cfg['tsl']`, gets `undefined`, and continues. `connect()` then dials with no CA configured and TLS silently falls back to system roots — the exact 'misspelled key leaves the built-in default in place while the operator believes they replaced it' outcome the doc promises to refuse. `nested` is typed `Readonly<Record<string, readonly string[]>>`, so the compiler does not relate its keys to `keys`.
remediation: Fail fast on the DECLARATION: at the top of `assertKnownConfigKeys`, throw if any `Object.keys(declared.nested ?? {})` is missing from `declared.keys`. Tighten the type in the same edit where possible — `nested?: Partial<Record<K, readonly string[]>>` with `keys: readonly K[]` — so the common case is a compile error and the runtime check catches the widened-type callers.
testUpgrade: Give this module a test IN core (it currently has none — mutating away the top-level check, the nested check and the non-object check each left all 3283 bridge-core tests green; only the ten backend suites and packages/conformance catch them). Parameterize over MALFORMED DECLARATIONS as a class: a nested key absent from `keys`; an empty `keys`; a nested member list that is empty — each asserted to throw from the declaration rather than to pass silently. Pair with the existing repo-wide conformance rows so the module is graded where it lives as well as where it is consumed.

remediationCheck.reliesOn: the existing `refuse()` helper and the top-level loop's `declared.keys.includes(key)` check; the new assertion runs before either and calls neither.
remediationCheck.newlyRejects: a plugin whose `BackendConfigKeys` declares a `nested` key it does not also list in `keys`. I grepped all ten backends: only bridge-nats declares `nested` (`tls`), and `tls` is present in its `keys`, so no shipped plugin is newly rejected.
remediationCheck.testsThatWouldFail: none found. I applied the nested-check mutation and ran `packages/bridge-nats/test/config.test.ts`: 12 tests failed, so nats' `tls.ca_flie` rows do cover the nested branch today and are unaffected by adding a declaration check. bridge-core's own 3283 tests are unaffected either way, which is the gap.
remediationCheck.hidesOrFixes: The declaration check makes the typo loud, but it does not make the nested walk recursive — a THIRD level (`a.b.c`) is still unvalidated, which the doc does not claim and no caller uses today.

Nothing in packages/ imports `startFakeOidc` from '@sharptrick/parley-core' — the front-doors fixture imports it relatively.

summary: The only test that grades `filterReachable`'s FAIR-SHARE rule builds its pressure from wall-clock cost, and that cost collapses ~100x once V8 is warm. Mutating `budget()` from per-entry fair share back to whole-call first-come — the exact regression the 12-line comment in presence-reach.ts:36-45 exists to prevent — leaves the ENTIRE package green (3283/3283). The 21-case `describe('a hostile presence page cannot silently delete a reachable peer')` block discriminates nothing in a normal run.
failure: Apply `const share = PATTERN_BUDGET_MS - spentMs;` (first-come) at presence-reach.ts:49. `npx vitest run packages/bridge-core` -> 3283 passed. `npx vitest run packages/bridge-core/src/transport/list-users-tool.test.ts` (whole file) -> 65 passed. Only `-t 'a hostile subset spends only its share'` in isolation goes red. Measured in-file warm cost of the pressure the test builds: ONE entry's full 64-source `costlyBank` = 0.45 ms, four entries = 1.54 ms — against a 50 ms allowance. The test comment asserts "ONE entry's full bank of costly sources already outspends the allowance several times over"; it is short by ~100x. `presence.test.ts:760` ('cannot starve the other direction') cannot cover the gap either: its shape sets `patterns: 0`, so the inbound `peerReach` budget is never spent at all.
remediation: Stop deriving the pressure from the clock. Add an injectable budget to `filterReachable`'s options (`patternBudgetMs`, defaulting to `PATTERN_BUDGET_MS`) and thread it from `list-users-tool.ts`; then pin the sharing rule with a deterministic budget small enough that the first entry provably exhausts it, and assert the peer BEHIND the saturating prefix is still returned. Keep one clock-based cell as a smoke test but stop treating it as the grader. Additionally, make the existing test self-verifying: measure `matchCost` of the bank it builds (presence.test.ts already has that helper) and `expect` it to exceed a stated fraction of the allowance, so a bank that stops costing anything reddens instead of passing.
testUpgrade: Guard the class 'a budget/allowance test whose pressure is timing-derived and therefore unfalsifiable when warm': parameterize the sharing rule over (budgetMs injected, saturating-prefix length, benign-peer position in {first, middle, last}) with the budget INJECTED rather than raced, so every cell fails deterministically under a first-come, a shared-across-directions, or a no-clip budget. Pair it with a meta-assertion — in every suite that constructs 'expensive' untrusted input, assert the constructed input's measured cost against the bound it is supposed to exceed, so a corpus that stops being expensive reddens rather than silently passing. `presence.test.ts:760` and `list-users-tool.test.ts:736` are both too narrow to have caught this: the first zeroes the inbound factor, the second only asserts disclosure.

remediationCheck.reliesOn: `presence-reach.ts` `budget(onClipped)` closure and the module-private `const PATTERN_BUDGET_MS = 50`; `filterReachable`'s options bag (currently `{scope, canPostTo, mySubscribedTopics, onReachClipped}`); `presence.test.ts`'s existing `matchCost(src)` helper at line 598.
remediationCheck.newlyAccepts: none in production — the default stays PATTERN_BUDGET_MS, so production behaviour is unchanged.
remediationCheck.newlyRejects: a future edit that makes the allowance first-come, whole-call, or shared across the two directions — all three are green today.
remediationCheck.testsThatWouldFail: none found. I checked every call site of `filterReachable` (presence.test.ts lines 473, 743, 750, 769, 923, 933, 943, 945, 960, 969, 988, 997, 1029, 1033, 1047, 1050, 1063, 1069 and list-users-tool.ts:126); they all pass an object literal with no `satisfies`/exact-type constraint, so an added optional key compiles everywhere.
remediationCheck.hidesOrFixes: Nothing stays broken: the production sharing rule is CORRECT today. What is broken is the detector — if a later round rewrites `budget()`, the suite will report success. Applying only the meta-assertion (measuring the corpus cost) without injecting the budget would still leave the sharing rule graded by a race.

summary: `MAX_HANDLE_LEN` (128) is enforced in `decodePresence` only on the SELF-REPORTED `handle`. `emitterOf` falls back to `m.senderHandle` for a beat that omits the field — the documented mixed-version compatibility path — and that fallback is capped nowhere. An unbounded string becomes a roster map key, is returned verbatim by `parley_list_users` into the agent's context, and is fed to `globMatch`'s O(pattern x value) walk.
failure: Post to the presence topic a v2 beat with NO `handle` key — `{"v":2,"kind":"hello","at":<now>,"topics":["ctx"],"postTopics":[]}` — from a sender whose display name is 1,000,000 characters. Probe run against `computeRoster([m], now, {ttlMs:90000, sinceMs:600000})` printed: `roster entries 1 handle length 1000000 cap 128`. The record is NOT dropped and NOT truncated. The mirror case — a beat that DOES carry a 129-char `handle` — is dropped whole (stated-bounds.test.ts:462). One 1 MB entry survives `filterHandles` at O(256 x 1e6) char comparisons per filtered peer, and up to MAX_ROSTER_ENTRIES=128 such entries can be returned in one `parley_list_users` answer.
remediation: Apply the same drop-not-truncate policy at the fallback. Make `emitterOf` return `undefined` when `rec.handle === undefined && m.senderHandle.length > MAX_HANDLE_LEN`, and `continue` the fold loop on that — mirroring `decodePresence`'s `if (handle !== undefined && handle.length > MAX_HANDLE_LEN) return null;`. Do not truncate: truncation would merge two peers sharing a 128-char prefix into one roster entry, which is exactly the hazard presence.test.ts:825 was written to pin.
testUpgrade: Guard the class 'a documented cap enforced on the primary field but not on its compatibility fallback'. Widen the existing `stated-bounds.test.ts` MAX_HANDLE_LEN row and presence.test.ts:833 ('two records differing only past the %s cap are never merged') into a table over (field-source in {self-reported `handle`, backend `senderHandle` fallback}) x (at cap, one past cap) and require the SAME verdict from both sources. Same shape for MAX_INSTANCE_ID_LEN and any future field with a fallback. A generator that fuzzes `senderHandle` length alongside `handle` length would also catch inputs I did not try.

remediationCheck.reliesOn: `decodePresence`'s existing branch `if (handle !== undefined && handle.length > MAX_HANDLE_LEN) return null;` (presence-beat.ts:142) as the policy precedent, and `computeRoster`'s `if (rec === null) continue;` loop-skip (presence.ts:145) as the place a dropped record already exits.
remediationCheck.newlyRejects: a pre-`handle`-field beat whose BACKEND sender exceeds 128 characters — today such a peer appears in the roster. On a backend where legitimate sender ids are long (a full Matrix MXID is well under 128; a raw JID is too), this would silently remove a real peer, so the cap value should be re-checked against the longest legitimate `senderHandle` a shipped plugin emits before landing.
remediationCheck.testsThatWouldFail: none found — and here is where I looked. summary: `startPushLoop` re-checks `subscribed.has(m.topic)` and calls it "a trust boundary, not a redundancy", citing DESIGN §14: "the bridge only ever surfaces the topics it was configured for, and never a presence beat". `parley_fetch_recent` performs no such check — it serialises `result.messages` verbatim. A plugin whose history read is coarser than a topic (the same NATS-wildcard / Matrix-room coarseness the push comment names) puts unallowed topics, including the reserved presence topic, straight into the agent's context.
failure: With `topics: ['ctx']` and a plugin whose `fetchRecent` returns messages tagged `ctx`, `secret-ops` and `parley-presence`, calling `parley_fetch_recent {topic: 'ctx'}` returned all three. The `parley_list_users` tool description simultaneously promises callers "except the reserved presence topic, which is refused even when a pattern covers it" (tool-schema.ts:23), which the pull path does not deliver. Secondary corruption: `deps.seen?.markSeen(t, m.backendMsgId)` at tools.ts:146 records the FOREIGN messages' ids under the REQUESTED topic `t`, so a genuine live push on `ctx` carrying a colliding `backendMsgId` is then suppressed by `firstSeen`.

Log once per handler invocation (not per message, and not keyed by the untrusted topic string) when anything was dropped, mirroring push-loop.ts's single `warned` flag.

Build a shared table over (delivery path in {live push, `parley_fetch_recent`, `parley_list_users`}) x (payload topic in {the requested topic, an unconfigured topic, a pattern-allowed-but-unsubscribed topic, the reserved presence topic}) and assert the SAME verdict at every path — the agent never sees a message whose `topic` is not the one it asked for. Add the coarse-delivery plugin to `testing/nonconformant.ts` so every backend's conformance run inherits it. The existing push-loop.test.ts case at line 299 is too narrow: it grades only the push path.

THE CONCRETE WAY THIS FIX CAN BE WORSE THAN THE BUG: if any plugin normalises `Message.topic` differently from the string the caller passed (case-folding, a `safeName` hash, a room-alias round-trip), the filter empties every page and `fetch_recent` silently returns nothing on a working topic. I checked `packages/bridge-matrix/src/wire.ts:124`, `packages/bridge-slack/src/markup.ts:78` and `packages/bridge-nats/src/payload.ts:18` — all three pass the caller's `topic` through to `buildMessage` unchanged — but I did not check every shipped plugin, so this must be verified across all of them before landing, or the filter must compare post-`allow.assert` normalised forms on both sides.

summary: `fetchRecent` calls `recordCatchUp` on BOTH arms, but its JSDoc premise — "the row `nextCursor` names, which is the caller's persisted read position" — only holds for the resuming (`since`) arm. A since-less read serves the NEWEST `limit` rows and then advances the live hand-off point to the topic tail, so `subscribe` starts above rows that no read returned and no caller persisted. Those rows are delivered by neither path.
failure: Reproduced against a real store (two SqlitePlugin instances on one file). reader.fetchRecent({topic,since:'0',limit:2}) serves old-0,old-1 and records hand-off=2. Peer commits window-0..window-4. reader.fetchRecent({topic,limit:1}) — a since-less read, exactly what the `parley_fetch_recent` tool issues with no `since` — returns only window-4 and raises the hand-off to rowid 7. reader.subscribe(...) then starts at 7. PUSHED: ["after-subscribe"]. A peer resuming from the cursor the caller actually persisted returns ["window-0","window-1","window-2","window-3","window-4","after-subscribe"]. window-0..3 are silently lost from live push. Reachable through the shipped CLI: transport/stdio-bridge.ts awaits server.connect(transport) (tools become answerable) BEFORE await startPushLoop(...), so a fetch_recent call landing in that window does this to a topic a peer is writing.
remediation: The correct fix is a seam change: the resume point for the live loop is something only core knows (it owns read-state), so it should be passed in — `subscribe(topic, handler, { since })` — rather than inferred by the plugin from a read whose purpose it cannot see. Surface that rather than absorbing it. The in-plugin narrowing that closes the reachable case without touching core is to record from the since-less arm only when the topic has no ledger entry (the cold-start case core's catchUpTopic actually uses): `if (resumeAfter !== undefined || !this.caughtUpThrough.has(args.topic)) this.recordCatchUp(...)`.
testUpgrade: catchup-live-handoff.test.ts's READ_PLANS matrix is the right home but every one of its four plans reads with an explicit `since` (`fromTheStart`), so the since-less arm of fetchRecent is not a row anywhere in the hand-off grade — that is the coverage gap that let this class through. Add the read SHAPE as a dimension: {resuming-since, since-less, since-less-after-a-resuming-read, no-read-at-all} x SHAPES x WINDOW_SIZES, with the invariant stated once and independently of the plan — `pushed` must equal what `peer.fetchRecent({since: <the cursor the plan handed the caller>})` returns, plus the post-subscribe row. That formulation catches any future read path that moves the ledger past rows the caller was never given, not just this one.

remediationCheck.reliesOn: `this.caughtUpThrough` (the Map declared in SqliteCatchUp) and the existing `const resumeAfter = args.since === undefined ? undefined : this.resumeAfter(...)` branch immediately above; the narrowing depends on `resumeAfter !== undefined` being exactly "the caller supplied a since", which it is.
remediationCheck.newlyAccepts: none — no input is newly accepted or rejected; only the ledger write is suppressed.
remediationCheck.newlyRejects: none
remediationCheck.testsThatWouldFail: Exactly one, verified by applying the patch and running bounded-state + catchup-live-handoff + conformance (143 cases): `test/bounded-state.test.ts > the catch-up hand-off survives until its topic is evicted > a topic whose hand-off keeps advancing outlives a flood of topics fetched once`. That test asserts ['between','after'] precisely because a second since-less read advanced the hand-off — i.e. the suite currently pins the defect, which is itself worth adjudicating. Conformance stayed green on both drivers.
remediationCheck.hidesOrFixes: With the patch the repro pushes exactly the owed set (verified: PUSHED == OWED). What it does NOT fix, and what the seam change would: the ledger is still a heuristic about the caller's intent, not a fact. A caller that pages with `since` but never persists the cursor it gets back still moves the hand-off past rows it will not re-read. If the bug were left in place and only this patch applied, nothing would be hidden — the residual is a narrower version of the same class.
remediationCheck.interleavings: n/a — the exposure is a request-ordering window (server.connect -> tool call -> startPushLoop) rather than a data race; the patch adds no new shared state and no new await point.

summary: SqlitePlugin is the tip of a five-level chain — SqliteStore <- SqliteCatchUp <- SqliteRetention <- SqlitePoller <- SqlitePlugin — in which every level has exactly one subclass and nothing is ever substituted for anything. Inheritance is being used to split one class across five files, paying for it with `protected` state reachable across four levels and with `Object.assign(this, prepared)` writing prepared statements into fields declared two levels away. This is the single-variant abstraction the design lens asks to be flagged as firmly as a missing seam.
failure: Not a runtime failure — a comprehension and blast-radius cost that is visible in the tests: to grade a poll loop, test/subscription-health.test.ts and test/background-jobs.test.ts must reach through `p as unknown as { selectAfterStmt: Stmt }` into a field declared in SqliteStore, four levels below the class under test, and swap it. Every test in the package that touches the poll loop, the prune or the plan check does the same cast. There is no interface at any level; the chain buys no polymorphism and no test seam, only file boundaries.
remediation: Collapse to one class (the files can stay as free functions plus a single class, or the concerns can be held as composed collaborators the plugin owns — a Poller, a Pruner — each constructed with the driver and the prepared statements it needs). The seam that matters is BackendPlugin, and it is already there. Do NOT introduce interfaces per level to justify the chain; that would add the variance the code does not have.

A repo-level meta-test over `packages/*/src/**/*.ts` that, for every `export abstract class X` (or every class named in an `extends` clause), asserts more than one distinct subtype exists in the workspace — written as an import-graph query over the parsed sources, not a per-file path assertion, so it stays true after a decomposition moves the files. Existing tests cannot catch this class at all: bounded-state.test.ts walks `Object.entries(p)` and sees the flattened instance, which is identical either way.

remediationCheck.reliesOn: The chain's own `protected` members: driver, pollIntervalMs, stopped, generation, storeId, the six *Stmt fields, tornDown(), orphaned(), require(), caughtUpThrough, retentionDays, pruneTimer, pruneBatchTimer, pruneFailures, lastPruneDiag, cancellers, health. All of these are already one flat instance at runtime, so a collapse changes no field name and no `this` shape.
remediationCheck.newlyRejects: none
remediationCheck.testsThatWouldFail: None from the casts, since every `p as unknown as { … }` reads a field on the same instance regardless of which class declares it, and bounded-state's Object.entries walk is shape-identical. What WOULD need updating: test/typecheck-coverage.test.ts enumerates `src/**` and asserts every .ts is inside a tsconfig project (adding or removing files is fine, it globs), and test/publish-hygiene.test.ts's `emittedFrom('src')` likewise globs — so neither pins the file list. summary: `assertMintedCursor` interpolates the caller's `since` into its error verbatim — unbounded and unsanitized. `since` is not a plugin-minted value: `parley_fetch_recent`'s schema is `z.string().optional()` (bridge-core/src/transport/tools.ts:93), so any MCP client — the model, or a remote chat peer in the OAuth deployment — fully controls it. The resulting Error is thrown out of the seam, rendered by core as an `isError` tool result (model context) and written by cli.ts to stderr. This package already declares the exact opposite invariant for server text (`fromServer` -> `sanitizeBody`, graded across 98 rows in hostile-server.test.ts); the cursor is a second untrusted-text channel into the identical sinks with no guard at all.

The cursor rows need no server (assertMintedCursor throws before `require()`), so they join the ungated half. live-stream.test.ts's `foreign` cursor table is the existing test too narrow to catch this: every one of its 13 rows is a short printable string and it asserts only that the message matches `/malformed cursor .* for topic/`.

summary: `passwordSpellings` reads only `new URL(url).password`, so the redaction sweep is blind to a credential in the USERNAME position. node-redis sends AUTH whenever username OR password is set (@redis/client/dist/lib/client/index.js:404-406) and puts the decoded username on the wire, and Redis echoes the arguments it was given back inside `unknown command '<cmd>', with args beginning with: '<arg>'`. The plugin itself already classifies a bare username as a credential — `reportPlaintextCredential` fires on `parsed.username !== ''` and warns that 'the AUTH this bridge sends … crosses the network in the clear' — so the two halves of the package disagree about what a credential is.
failure: `connect({url: 'redis://hunter2@<host>:<port>'})` against a server that echoes its arguments -> fake observed AUTH args `["hunter2",""]` and the plugin threw `parley-redis: connected to 127.0.0.1:38961 but the server refused a command: ERR unknown command 'AUTH', with args beginning with: 'hunter2', '',` — the credential verbatim, into stderr and into the model context core builds from the thrown seam error. Reproduced against the package's own `respEndpoint` fake.

Keep it conditional on the empty password: with `redis://<user>:<pw>@host` the username is an ACL name, and Redis's canonical spelling of that name is `default`, so an unconditional sweep would replace the word 'default' throughout every server message.

summary: `entryTimestamp`'s clamp is `ms >= 0 && ms <= MAX_DATE_MS`. Its own comment justifies only the UPPER bound (a uint64 stream-id millisecond past what `Date` can represent would throw `RangeError` out of the seam). The lower bound has no such justification: `Date` represents instants down to -8.64e15, so every entry whose `ts` field names a pre-1970 instant is silently rewritten to `1970-01-01T00:00:00.000Z` instead of being reported. A stream id's millisecond component is digits-only and can never be negative, so the guard only ever fires on the `ts` path, where it is wrong.
failure: An entry written by any peer or by redis-cli as `XADD <key> * sender alice content hi ts 1900-01-01T00:00:00.000Z` comes back from both `fetchRecent` and `subscribe` with `timestamp === '1970-01-01T00:00:00.000Z'` — a value that is well-formed ISO 8601 and 70 years wrong, with no diagnostic. Reproduced directly through `rowToMessage`.
remediation: Make the clamp symmetric: `ms >= -MAX_DATE_MS && ms <= MAX_DATE_MS`. That preserves the RangeError guard the comment is actually about while letting a representable instant through.
testUpgrade: The class is 'the ts axis is graded only on one side of an arithmetic boundary'. live-stream.test.ts's `foreignEntries` table has 14 rows and every `from-ts` row names a post-1970 instant, so the lower clamp is ungraded in BOTH directions — I widened it to `-MAX_DATE_MS` and the whole package stayed green. Derive the `ts` rows from `Date`'s own range the way the sibling `foreignIds` table already derives ids from the uint64 bound: `{-LAST_DATE_MS, -LAST_DATE_MS+1, -1, 0, 1, LAST_DATE_MS-1, LAST_DATE_MS, LAST_DATE_MS+1}` rendered as ISO where representable, each asserted on both the fetchRecent and subscribe paths, with the expected value computed from the input rather than declared per row.

remediationCheck.reliesOn: `MAX_DATE_MS = 8_640_000_000_000_000` in the same file, and on `new Date(-8.64e15).toISOString()` being legal (it is: that is the first representable instant, `-271821-04-20T00:00:00.000Z`).
remediationCheck.newlyAccepts: An entry whose `ts` parses to a negative millisecond now reports that instant instead of the epoch — e.g. `ts: '1900-01-01T00:00:00.000Z'` becomes `1900-01-01T00:00:00.000Z`.
remediationCheck.newlyRejects: none. `Date.parse` returning NaN still takes the id fallback, and a millisecond below -MAX_DATE_MS still falls to 0 rather than throwing.
remediationCheck.testsThatWouldFail: none found. I applied exactly this edit and ran the whole package against a live Redis: 798 green. I looked at every timestamp assertion — live-stream.test.ts:72 and :185 compute the expected value as `new Date(source).toISOString()` from the row's own input, so a pre-1970 row would follow the fix rather than fight it, and no existing row is pre-1970.
remediationCheck.hidesOrFixes: If applied while some other timestamp defect remained, it would still be true that a `ts` below -8.64e15 (only reachable from a hand-written `ts`, not from an id) silently becomes 1970 rather than being rejected — the clamp is a fallback, not a validation, and this fix does not change that.

summary: `assertStorable` screens encoding hazards (NUL, unpaired surrogate) but not SIZE, and `post()`/`resolveIdentity()` only rename two error shapes (pg's 'Query read timeout' and SQLSTATE 55P03). A `topic` or handle whose bytes do not compress past PostgreSQL's ~2704-byte btree item limit is refused by the server with SQLSTATE 54000, and the raw driver string — including the internal index name — is what the caller gets. `subscribe()` on the same topic succeeds, so the live path registers for a topic no post can ever land in.
failure: Against postgres:16-alpine: `post(asTopic(<3000 random printable ASCII chars>), asHandle('u'), 'hi')` rejects with `index row size 3024 exceeds btree version 4 maximum 2704 for index "parley_long_aoxfmf_topic_seq"`; `resolveIdentity(asHandle(<3000 chars>))` rejects with `index row size 3016 exceeds btree version 4 maximum 2704 for index "parley_long_hfcj6c_senders_pkey"`. Neither names this plugin, the field, nor 'nothing was written', and both disclose the deployment's relation name into agent context. `subscribe(<same 3000-char topic>)` resolves ok.
remediation: Two parts. (1) Add a byte-budget screen beside the encoding screen for the two fields that reach a btree key — `topic` (via `<table>_topic_seq`) and `handle` (via `<table>_senders_pkey`) — refusing with the same `parley-postgres: invalid <field> — … Nothing was written` shape, and apply it in post/fetchRecent/subscribe/resolveIdentity wherever assertStorable already runs, so subscribe and post agree on what a usable topic is. The budget must sit under 2704 minus index-tuple overhead and the trailing `seq` key, not at 2704. (2) Make `post()`'s catch rename ANY server refusal, not just 55P03 and the read timeout: `answerAbandoned`/`lockWaitAbandoned` both fall through with `return err as Error`, so every other SQLSTATE (54000, 53100 disk full, 42501 permission denied) reaches agent context bare.
testUpgrade: Guard the class 'a field the server refuses for a reason this plugin never anticipated must still come back as a parley-postgres: message'. In test/storable-corpus.ts add REFUSED rows generated at a parameterized set of byte lengths spanning the boundary — e.g. 2_600, 2_704, 2_705, 4_096, 8_192 — built from INCOMPRESSIBLE bytes (a fixed-seed random printable generator), so a future limit change moves which row fires rather than silencing the rule; hostile-input.test.ts already crosses every seam call with every field, so the new rows inherit the full matrix. Separately, parameterize a real-server case over induced SQLSTATEs (revoke INSERT for 42501; oversized index key for 54000) asserting `/^parley-postgres: /` and `/[Nn]othing was written/` on the rejection. The existing corpus cannot catch this: its only long value is `'x'.repeat(1MiB)`, which `indexableFields` routes to `content` alone.

remediationCheck.reliesOn: `assertStorable(field, value)` and its call sites in index.ts (post lines 272-275, fetchRecent 311, subscribe 345, resolveIdentity 419); `answerAbandoned`'s branch `if (!answerNeverCame(err)) return err as Error;` (errors.ts:113) and `lockWaitAbandoned`'s `if ((err as {code?: string})?.code !== LOCK_NOT_AVAILABLE) return err as Error;` (errors.ts:130) — these two pass-throughs are exactly why the 54000 arrives bare.
remediationCheck.newlyRejects: `post`/`subscribe`/`fetchRecent` with a topic over the budget, and `resolveIdentity`/`post` with a handle over it — today these reach the server (topic/handle) or, for subscribe, silently succeed.
remediationCheck.testsThatWouldFail: none found, and here is where I looked: storable-roundtrip.test.ts routes its only long value (1 MiB) to `content` via `indexableFields`, so a topic/handle budget does not touch it; hostile-input.test.ts's corpus values are all short; notify-channel.test.ts's longest topic is 500 chars; conformance.test.ts's `freshTopic()` is under 40 chars; table-name.test.ts bounds table_name, not topic. I read each of these.
remediationCheck.hidesOrFixes: If only part (2) is applied, the error is named but a topic an operator listed in `topics` is still one `subscribe()` succeeds on and every `post()` fails on — the asymmetry survives. If only part (1) is applied, every other SQLSTATE (permission denied, disk full) still reaches agent context as a bare PostgreSQL string.

summary: `INDEX_KEY_MAX_BYTES = 8191` and its comment ('PostgreSQL refuses a btree index row over 8191 bytes, and `topic`, `sender` and `in_reply_to` are all index keys in this schema') are both false. The measured ceiling is 2704, and neither `sender` nor `in_reply_to` is an index key in buildSchema — the only indexes are `(topic, seq)`, `(created_at)` and `_senders(handle)`. `indexableFields` therefore routes values the server will refuse into the `topic` and `handle` cells, and mislabels `inReplyTo` as constrained. It is invisible only because no corpus row lands in 2705..8191.
failure: `indexableFields(<3000 incompressible chars>)` returns `["content","topic","handle","inReplyTo"]`, so a corpus row of that length in the ROUND_TRIPS arm would be driven into storable-roundtrip's `topic` and `handle` cells and fail against a real server with SQLSTATE 54000. Conversely an 8000-byte `in_reply_to` posts and stores fine (measured), so the splitter also excludes cells the server would happily hold.
remediation: Set the splitter from the real btree item limit (2704, minus index-tuple overhead) rather than from the page size, and derive WHICH fields are constrained from `buildSchema`'s index list — `topic` and `handle` only — instead of restating a set by hand. Then, once the plugin gains a size screen, move the boundary values into the REFUSED arm so the two files grade opposite halves of the same fact.
testUpgrade: Guard the class 'a test helper that decides which cells run must not encode a server fact nobody re-measures'. Replace the literal with a value the suite MEASURES once against the live server in a beforeAll (post a binary-searched incompressible topic until 54000), and assert `INDEX_KEY_MAX_BYTES` equals it — so the constant cannot drift from the server the suite is actually running on. Pair it with a parameterized boundary corpus (2_600 / 2_704 / 2_705 / 8_191 / 8_192) so the splitter is exercised on both sides of its own threshold instead of only far above it.

remediationCheck.reliesOn: `indexableFields` (storable-corpus.ts:77) and its single consumer, storable-roundtrip.test.ts:29-31 `CORPUS.filter(...).flatMap(([label, value]) => indexableFields(value).map(...))`; also storable-roundtrip.test.ts:46-51, which asserts the produced cells cover all four field names.
remediationCheck.newlyAccepts: `inReplyTo` cells for values in 2705..8191, which the current splitter would have excluded once the constant is corrected — correct, since in_reply_to is not indexed.
remediationCheck.newlyRejects: `topic`/`handle` cells for values in 2705..8191, which today are generated and would fail.
remediationCheck.testsThatWouldFail: storable-roundtrip.test.ts:46 'there are cells to run, and they cover every field the seam takes' asserts the cell set covers all four fields — if the corrected splitter is applied while the only long value is the 1 MiB one, coverage is unchanged (that value already routes to `content` alone), so this case still passes. summary: `destroySocket` reaches for `resource.connection.stream.destroy()`. `pg.Client` has that path; `pg.Pool` does not (`new Pool(...).connection === undefined`, verified). So `endWithin(pool, …)` — the call `disconnect()` makes for the query pool and for every in-flight bootstrap pool — gives up after the budget and destroys nothing. The README's 'destroying a connection that will not close rather than waiting on a FIN that is not coming' and the function's own 'so that a bounded teardown does not trade a hung shutdown for a live connection' are true only of the listener Client.
failure: Through a TCP proxy that swallows data and FIN in both directions: connect + post (releases a pooled client), blackhole, issue a second post (parks holding a checkout), then `disconnect()`. disconnect resolves in 5255 ms as advertised, but `pool._clients` still holds one client with `connection.stream.destroyed === false` at t+5255, t+9259 and t+13264 ms; it only goes away at ~15 s when `query_timeout` finally rejects the parked statement. For that window a socket and its server backend outlive a teardown the caller was told had completed.
remediation: Either narrow the claim to what the code can do — say the listener socket is destroyed and the pooled ones are bounded by `connectionTimeoutMillis`/`query_timeout` instead — or extend `destroySocket` to walk a Pool's clients (`(resource as {_clients?: Closeable[]})._clients`) under the same every-hop-optional discipline the function already uses, so a driver that renames the field degrades to today's behaviour rather than throwing inside `disconnect()`. Do not claim both.
testUpgrade: Guard the class 'the give-up path of a bounded teardown really closes the resource, for EVERY resource type this plugin ends'. Parameterize a real-socket case over {listener Client, query Pool} x {idle at teardown, checked out and parked}, asserting after `await disconnect()` that no socket the plugin opened is still `destroyed === false` — reached through the resource the plugin holds rather than through a hard-coded private path, so a fifth resource added later is covered by construction. Today silent-peer.test.ts asserts only that disconnect RESOLVES and in what order, which is why reducing destroySocket to `return;` left all 1011 tests green.

remediationCheck.reliesOn: `endWithin` (connection.ts:84) calling `destroySocket(resource)` after `settledWithin(ended, budgetMs)` returns false; `Closeable` is only `{ end: () => Promise<unknown> }`, so the Pool branch has to be a cast the same way the Client branch already is.
remediationCheck.newlyRejects: none — behavioural only, on the give-up path.
remediationCheck.testsThatWouldFail: none found — I proved the opposite directly: replacing the whole body of destroySocket with `return;` kept 36/36 files and 1011/1011 tests green, so nothing in the package grades this path in either direction.
remediationCheck.hidesOrFixes: If only the README/comment is narrowed and the code is left alone, a pooled socket still outlives a resolved `disconnect()` by up to QUERY_WAIT_MS (15 s) — bounded, but the process cannot exit cleanly in that window, which is the property the ceiling exists for. If only the code is extended, the destroy has to tolerate a client mid-handshake; I did not trace pg-pool's behaviour when a client it is still dialling is destroyed underneath it, so treat that half as untested.

summary: A kick/ban (or any loss of room membership) makes the subscribe loop silently deaf forever: /sync keeps answering 200, the room simply stops appearing under rooms.join, and the loop reads `json.rooms?.join?.[roomId]?.timeline` as `undefined`, delivers nothing, resets consecutiveFailures to 0, logs nothing and keeps long-polling at full rate. `rooms.leave` is never read anywhere in src/. Both the README ('A failing /sync (revoked token, kick, homeserver fault) is reported on stderr and retried with exponential backoff up to 30s — never a silent hot loop') and diagnostics.ts's JSDoc ('kicked from the room → 403') assert this is reported; /sync never 403s for a kick.
failure: Reproduced with a throwaway test against FakeSynapse: subscribe('ops'), then every incremental /sync answers 200 with `{ rooms: { leave: {} } }` (no join block), then a peer posts 'after-the-kick'. Result: handler received [], console.error received zero calls, fake.syncAttempts kept climbing at the un-backed-off rate. Wrong output: live delivery is permanently dead and the operator gets no signal at all — only fetchRecent still 403s loudly, so the read path is loud and the live path is mute, the exact inverse of what the README claims.
remediation: In the subscribe loop, after `nextBatchOf`, read `json.rooms?.leave?.[roomId]`; when present, report it on stderr via a dedicated diagnostic naming the topic, the room and the fix (re-invite the account), and throw into the existing catch so the backoff ladder engages (the next iteration's ensureRoom/join can then recover a re-invited account). Do NOT key on absence from `rooms.join` — an incremental /sync legitimately omits a room with no new events, so that spelling would report every idle poll as a failure. Correspondingly amend the README sentence and diagnostics.ts's '(revoked token → 401, kicked from the room → 403)' parenthetical, which is factually wrong about /sync.

remediationCheck.reliesOn: The existing `catch (err) { if (this.isStale(generation)) break; consecutiveFailures++; reportSyncFailure(...); await this.interruptibleDelay(syncRetryDelayMs(...)); continue; }` block in index.ts:242-251, and the `/sync` filter `{ room: { rooms: [roomId], … } }` in wire.ts:40 — a RoomFilter's `rooms` whitelist applies to the leave section too, so `rooms.leave[roomId]` is reachable under this filter.
remediationCheck.newlyRejects: A /sync body that lists this room under `rooms.leave` — today a 200 the loop treats as healthy and empty; after the fix it is a reported failure that backs off.
remediationCheck.testsThatWouldFail: none found — I grepped test/ for `rooms.leave` and `leave` and found none in any fake body; the only body that omits `join` is subscribe-resilience.fake.test.ts's BODY_FAULTS['the room is missing from rooms.join'], which is a POSITIONING-sync override and carries no `leave` key, so a leave-keyed check does not read it. Note that the naive absence-keyed spelling WOULD break that row, which is why the remediation names the distinction.
remediationCheck.hidesOrFixes: If applied while the loop still never inspects membership, nothing is hidden — the operator gets a stderr line and a backoff but delivery for that topic stays dead until the account is re-invited and ensureRoom re-joins. Recovery is a separate (and legitimate) follow-on; the finding is about the silence, and the fix ends the silence.
remediationCheck.interleavings: The check runs on the same synchronous path as the existing timeline read, inside the loop's try, so it cannot race the abort/staleness gates that already bracket it. Two callers on the new path: subscribe's loop and pollBoundedSync (which reads the same join block for a blocking fetchRecent) — pollBoundedSync is best-effort and bounded by blockMs, so leaving it unchanged keeps a kicked blocking read returning empty at its deadline rather than hanging.

testUpgrade: Give FakeSynapse a `membership` knob so a kick is expressible at all (today no fixture can produce one), then a parameterized table over MEMBERSHIP_LOSS shapes — room under `rooms.leave` with an `m.room.member` leave, the same with `ban`, a kick followed by a re-invite+re-join — crossed with the two live drivers (subscribe loop, dedicated /sync behind a blocking fetchRecent). Each row asserts (a) a stderr line naming the topic, (b) the retry cadence changes (syncAttempts spacing grows), and (c) delivery resumes after re-invite. The existing subscribe-resilience 'permanent /sync failure' rows are too narrow to have caught this: they only model an HTTP status or a rejected fetch, never a 200 that has stopped carrying the room.

summary: `connect()` does `const json = (await res.json()) as { access_token: string; user_id: string }` with no guard. wire.ts's own stated invariant is the opposite — 'Every field is member-controlled JSON on which the homeserver enforces no schema. Keep these `unknown`, so that no value reaches buildMessage without passing a guard' — and nextBatchOf/positioningBatchOf both throw on a bad shape. The login response, the one place the credential is minted, gets none of that.
failure: Reproduced with a stub fetch answering the login 200. (1) body `{}` or `{ user_id: '@parley:fake' }` → connect() RESOLVES; every later seam call throws `[parley-matrix] refusing PUT …: this plugin holds no access token … it is disconnected, or its last connect() did not complete its login`, which misdirects the operator to a disconnect that never happened. (2) body `null` → connect() rejects with a raw `TypeError: Cannot read properties of null (reading 'access_token')` at index.ts:72 — unlabelled, no `[parley-matrix]` prefix, naming neither the homeserver nor the login. (3) body `{ access_token: 12345 }` → `this.token = 12345` and `Authorization: Bearer 12345` goes on the wire for every subsequent request.
remediation: Read the body as `unknown`, narrow it, and reject a login that produced no usable credential: `if (typeof token !== 'string' || token === '') throw new Error('[parley-matrix] POST /_matrix/client/v3/login answered 200 for <baseUrl> but carried no access_token; this is not a Matrix homeserver, or a proxy/captive portal answered for it.')`. Set `this.userId` only when `user_id` is a string. `standDown()` has already run at the top of connect(), so the throw leaves the plugin credential-less, which is the state its later error message already assumes.

remediationCheck.reliesOn: `standDown()` at index.ts:50, which runs before the login and already clears `this.token`, so no partial state needs unwinding on the new throw path; and `this.http`'s existing credential-less refusal at session.ts:326, which stays the fallback for calls made before any connect().
remediationCheck.newlyRejects: A login that answers HTTP 200 with a body carrying no string `access_token` (JSON null, `{}`, a scalar, an array, a numeric token). Today all of these either resolve connect() or throw an unlabelled TypeError.
remediationCheck.testsThatWouldFail: none found — I grepped test/ for `access_token`: fake-synapse.ts:333, creds-warning.test.ts:14 and config-validation.test.ts:105 all mint a string token, and reconnect-lifecycle.fake.test.ts's `loginOutcome` axis only varies the HTTP status or rejects the fetch, never the 200 body. No fixture reaches the new branch.
remediationCheck.hidesOrFixes: If applied and something else still leaves `this.token` unset (say a future code path that clears it), the http() refusal at session.ts:326 keeps firing with its current misleading 'it is disconnected' wording — so the wording of that message is worth fixing in the same change, otherwise the fix only closes the connect()-time half.

testUpgrade: Add a `loginBody` override to FakeSynapse (sibling of the existing `loginOutcome`) and a parameterized table over LOGIN_BODIES — `{}`, JSON null, `[]`, a scalar, `{ user_id }` only, `{ access_token: 12345 }`, `{ access_token: '' }` — each asserting connect() rejects with a message carrying `[parley-matrix]` and the homeserver URL, and that no request afterwards carries an Authorization header. The class is 'an external response parsed by a bare `as` cast on a path that mints privilege'; widen it by asserting src/ contains no `as { access_token` / `as { room_id` / `as { event_id` style cast whose fields are then used unguarded, or by routing every response parse through one narrowing helper.

summary: `expect(PLUGIN_SRC).not.toMatch(/\/(?:leave|forget)`/)` — the guard whose own JSDoc says 'the day the plugin grows a leave, this fails so the paragraph is rewritten rather than left stale' — requires the path to be immediately followed by a backtick, i.e. spelled as the tail of a template literal. Any other spelling walks straight past it. This is exactly the CLAUDE.md standing rule against 'a regex that finds it in a particular file' rather than an import of a symbol.
failure: Mutated session.ts to add `protected async leaveRoom(roomId) { const path = '/_matrix/client/v3/rooms/' + encodeURIComponent(roomId) + '/leave'; await this.http('POST', path, { body: {} }); }` — shipped-artifacts.test.ts and comment-hygiene.test.ts stayed fully green (64 passed). Control: the same call written as a template literal ending in ``…/leave` `` DOES fail the guard (1 failed | 28 passed), so the hole is the spelling, not the whole assertion. A concatenated path, `` `…/leave?reason=x` ``, `` `…/forget` `` reached via a variable, or a helper in a new src/ subfile all ship a leave while the README paragraph about the ever-growing joined-room set stays green and stale.

Either (a) drive the invariant through behaviour — a table over every seam entry point asserting `fake.requestUrls` contains no path whose final segment is `leave` or `forget`, which is already how provisioning.fake.test.ts's SIDE_EFFECTS/WRITE_SHAPES table works and would classify a leave as an undeclared write; or (b) if a source scan is kept, match the path segment rather than its delimiter: `/['"`]\s*\+?[^'"`]*\/(?:leave|forget)(?![A-Za-z0-9_])/` over PLUGIN_SRC. (a) is strictly better — it survives a rename, a helper, and a new subdirectory.

remediationCheck.reliesOn: provisioning.fake.test.ts's `recordWrites(fake)` (line ~570), which already fails on any non-GET request not matching WRITE_SHAPES/PROBE_SHAPES — a `POST …/leave` would land in its `else` branch as `POST /_matrix/…/leave` and break the `toEqual(row.effects)` assertion. So option (a) is mostly already there and only needs the leave/forget segment named as forbidden rather than merely undeclared.
remediationCheck.newlyAccepts: A src/ file that mentions the word 'leave' in prose or a variable name without issuing the request — today the backtick form makes prose safe by accident, and a widened regex could catch it; the behavioural form (a) cannot.
remediationCheck.newlyRejects: A leave/forget request issued by any seam call, however its path string is built.
remediationCheck.testsThatWouldFail: none found — I ran shipped-artifacts.test.ts and comment-hygiene.test.ts against both the concatenated and the template-literal mutation; the unmutated tree passes either replacement, since src/ issues no leave today.
remediationCheck.hidesOrFixes: If applied while the plugin genuinely still never leaves a room, nothing changes operationally — the value is entirely in the guard firing the day a leave is added (which finding #4 below would add). Left as-is, that day arrives silently.

testUpgrade: Parameterize the class rather than the instance: a table of FORBIDDEN_ROOM_MUTATIONS = ['leave', 'forget', 'kick', 'ban', 'upgrade'] asserted from the WIRE (fake.requestUrls path segments) across every seam entry point, plus a self-check row that plants each spelling — template literal, string concatenation, a path held in a variable, a path with a query string — and asserts the guard fires for all of them. A guard whose own recogniser is not exercised at its boundary is the class; every regex-over-source lint in this package (the `/leave|forget` scan, `pluginMustNotMatch: /NoSuchTopicError/`, DEAD_REFERENCE) owes such a self-check.

summary: `adoptRoom` joins the room BEFORE reading its provenance (necessary — a non-member cannot read state), then throws when the creator or join rule fails the bar. The join is never undone: src/ contains no leave/forget. So a room the plugin explicitly REFUSES to use is nonetheless permanently added to the bridge account's joined-room set — the very set the README names as what bounds /sync latency ('a test fixture measured a session going from 3.4s to over 15s as rooms accumulated'). The topic driving the read comes from the model, whose context is fed by untrusted inbound messages.
failure: Trace: fetchRecent(topic) → existingRoom → lookupAlias resolves (the alias is deterministic and guessable, and the README says so) → adoptRoom → joinRoom succeeds (public_chat room, or one that invited us) → roomProvenance returns a stranger creator → throw. `this.rooms` is never populated, so the NEXT read of that topic repeats lookup + JOIN + state. An attacker who pre-claims `#parley_<topic>:<server_name>` for topics the allowlist admits by pattern gets the bridge account permanently joined to N attacker-controlled rooms, one per model-named topic, with every one of them refused — and each refusal costs the operator a further degraded /sync while producing no room the plugin will ever use. provisioning.fake.test.ts's 'a read of N distinct topics permanently joins N rooms' grades the accepted case; nothing grades the refused case.
remediation: On refusal in `adoptRoom`, issue a best-effort `POST /_matrix/client/v3/rooms/<id>/leave` before throwing (swallowing its own failure), so a room this session declines to use does not stay on the account. Then rewrite the README's 'Reads never provision — but they do JOIN' paragraph to say the plugin leaves a room it refuses, and update the shipped-artifacts guard accordingly.

remediationCheck.reliesOn: `this.http('POST', …, { body: {}, allowStatuses: [403, 404] })` — the leave must tolerate its own failure, since the account may already have been kicked; and on the fact that `this.rooms` was never populated for a refused room (session.ts:141 runs only after adoptRoom returns), so no cache entry needs invalidating.
remediationCheck.newlyRejects: none — the seam-visible outcome of a refused room is unchanged (the same throw, the same message).
remediationCheck.testsThatWouldFail: shipped-artifacts.test.ts > 'the plugin still never leaves or forgets a room, as that paragraph says' (line 402) fails on the template-literal spelling — I verified that control by hand. provisioning.fake.test.ts > 'a room the plugin did not create is adopted only on its stated trust bar' rows would also see a new POST …/leave; whether they fail depends on whether the case reaches recordWrites, which those rows do not use, but 'every seam call issues exactly the state changes it is declared to' does and would need a new declared shape if any of its rows started refusing. Both breakages are the correct signal: the README paragraph and the declared-side-effects table are precisely what this fix must move.
remediationCheck.hidesOrFixes: If applied while the JOIN still precedes the provenance read, the exposure window remains: the attacker still learns the bridge account joined (membership event, presence) before it leaves. Only the permanent accumulation is fixed. Nothing here is hidden by the fix — the throw is unchanged.
remediationCheck.interleavings: Two callers reach adoptRoom concurrently for the same alias (existingRoom from a read, resolveOrCreateRoom from a post): both may issue a leave; leave is idempotent (M_FORBIDDEN/404 tolerated). A leave racing a concurrent successful adopt of the SAME room by the other caller cannot happen, because both would compute the same provenance verdict from the same state.

testUpgrade: Widen provisioning.fake.test.ts's SIDE_EFFECTS table so every row declares the state changes of BOTH outcomes — the accepted room and the refused one — driven by a REFUSAL axis (stranger creator, disallowed join rule, unreadable state) crossed with the existing entry points, and assert `fake.rooms` membership rather than only the request log. Add a row 'a read of N topics whose aliases a stranger claimed leaves the account joined to 0 of them'. Today no case in the package asserts anything about the joined set after a refusal.

summary: `ensureRoom`'s failure handler is `.catch((err) => { this.rooms.delete(key); throw err; })` — it deletes whatever is at `key`, not the entry it inserted. Since `standDown()` clears `this.rooms` on every connect/disconnect, a resolve started under generation N that rejects AFTER generation N+1 has cached a good room for the same topic evicts the new generation's entry.
failure: Trace: gen1 `post(T)` → `rooms.set(T, pending1)`; `disconnect()` → `standDown()` → `rooms.clear()`; `connect()` → gen2; gen2 `post(T)` → `rooms.set(T, pending2)`, resolves and caches room R; then pending1 rejects (its in-flight http throws the credential refusal from session.ts:326, or its abort surfaces) → `this.rooms.delete(T)` removes pending2's entry. Wrong output: the next `post(T)`/`subscribe(T)` re-runs lookupAlias + join + GET /state for a room already resolved, and two concurrent first-posts after that eviction can both reach POST /createRoom, spending an extra unit of Synapse's ~1-room-per-45s per-user creation budget that the README treats as scarce. summary: `onOccupancyLost` returns without doing anything when `pendingJoins` holds the room. For a room this join CREATED, the pending entry survives the whole owner-config round trip (`onPresence` defers `pending.resolve()` behind `configureRoom`, an IQ with a 15 s timeout), so a kick/ban/destroy landing in that window is discarded entirely: no `forgetRoom`, no loss counted, no ladder armed, no stderr line — and the join then caches as RESOLVED for a room the connection is not in. `subscribe()` returns success and live push for that topic is dead forever (README: a catch-up-only room only re-enters on a later seam call; a subscribe-only topic never has one). The `subscribe()` JSDoc claims the opposite: 'an occupancy loss delivered inside the join ... is seen by onOccupancyLost as a subscribed room and arms the re-entry ladder'.
failure: subscribe(topic) on a brand-new room where the MUC answers status 201 and the owner-config submit takes ~300 ms, with the server sending `<presence type='unavailable'><x><status code='110'/><status code='307'/></x>` inside that window. Observed (probe run against FakeXmpp): {occupantOnServer: false, pluginThinksJoined: true, rejoinArmed: false, delivered: 0} — subscribe() resolved, the room routes us nothing, and no message ever reaches the handler.
remediation: Do not drop the loss — defer it until the in-flight join settles. In `onOccupancyLost`, replace the combined guard with: `if (!this.joined.has(room)) return; if (this.pendingJoins.has(room)) { this.joined.get(room)?.then(() => this.onOccupancyLost(room, why), () => undefined); return; }`. When the join resolves, `pendingJoins` is empty and `joined` still holds the room, so the normal forget + backoff + ladder path runs; when it rejects, `ensureJoinedRoom` has already forgotten the room and the caller saw the error, so nothing is owed.
testUpgrade: Guard the CLASS 'a room-state event delivered while the seam call that caused it is still in flight'. `membership-revalidation.test.ts` already has a `the loss lands $when` table for subscribe(); widen its `when` axis to a generator over the join's internal stages — {presence sent, self-presence delivered, room-created 201 + owner-config in flight, disco#info in flight, seam call returned} — crossed with the existing `losses` table (kick 307, ban 301, 321, 322, 332, destroy, silent forget + bounce). Every cell must end with the plugin an occupant again AND a message delivered through the handler (fake.deliverItem after the dust settles), never merely 'a join presence was sent'. FakeXmpp already has `announceCreation`, `ownerConfig`, `discoLatencyMs`, `onDiscoRequest` and `endOccupancy`; the missing knob is an owner-config LATENCY (today `ownerConfig` only accepts/refuses/times-out synchronously), which is what makes the widest cell reachable. `membership-revalidation.test.ts`'s current 'the loss lands $when' rows are too narrow because every one of them fires after `pendingJoins` is already empty.

remediationCheck.reliesOn: `this.joined.get(room)` — the ensure promise `ensureJoinedRoom` stores at line 245 (`const p = this.doJoin(room).then(() => this.assertMamAvailable(room)); this.joined.set(room, p);`). I depend on the branch where that promise RESOLVES: at that point `joinOnce`'s `settle()` has already run `this.pendingJoins.delete(room)`, so the recursive call falls through the `pendingJoins.has` guard. On the reject branch I deliberately do nothing, because `p.catch(() => { if (this.joined.get(room) === p) this.forgetRoom(room); })` at line 248 has already dropped the cache.
remediationCheck.newlyAccepts: An `<presence type='unavailable' from='room/ourNick'>` carrying 307/301/321/322/332/destroy that arrives between the join presence being sent and the join settling — today silently discarded, after the fix it forgets the room, logs `occupancy in <room> ended (...)` and arms the backoff ladder.
remediationCheck.newlyRejects: Nothing. No input that resolves today starts failing; `subscribe()`/`post()`/`fetchRecent()` return exactly as before, because the deferred work runs after their promise has already settled.
remediationCheck.testsThatWouldFail: None found. I applied this exact edit and ran the whole package against a live Prosody: 36 files / 1769 tests passed, and my probe went from red to green. I specifically watched membership-revalidation.test.ts ('recovers when $how', 'backs off instead of storming when $how', 'gives up loudly after a run of losses', 'does not treat its own nick change as losing the room'), rejoin-ladder.test.ts ('each loss waits its own step, jitter included, and then it gives up'), join-supersession.test.ts and pending-registry.test.ts — all still green.
remediationCheck.hidesOrFixes: It fixes the drop rather than hiding it. What is NOT fixed if the bug is otherwise left alone: two unavailable presences arriving inside one join window both defer and both count on settle, so the backoff ladder advances two steps for one round of trouble; and the loss's `at` timestamp is recorded at settle time rather than at loss time, so the REJOIN_WINDOW_MS 'recovered' judgement is measured from slightly late. Both are conservative (back off more, give up sooner), neither reopens the silent-death path.
remediationCheck.interleavings: Three orderings traced. (1) unavailable arrives, then the join resolves: defer fires on the resolve microtask, pendingJoins is empty, joined still has the room -> normal loss path. (2) The join REJECTS after the deferred hook is attached: the catch arm is a no-op and `ensureJoinedRoom`'s own `p.catch` has already called `forgetRoom`, so nothing double-forgets. (3) Two callers on the new path — a second `subscribe()`/`post()` for the same room awaiting the SAME cached `joined` promise, plus a second unavailable presence: both hooks attach to the one promise and both run `onOccupancyLost` after it settles; the first forgets the room and schedules a timer, the second re-enters with `joined.has(room)` now FALSE and returns at the first line, so exactly one ladder step is armed. `disconnect()` racing the window is covered by `onOccupancyLost`'s existing `if (this.stopped) return`, which the deferred call re-evaluates at fire time.

summary: The fixture's stanza-error constructor is `Object.assign(new Error(condition), { condition })` — `message` is IDENTICAL to `condition`. The real `@xmpp/error` (node_modules/@xmpp/error/index.js) builds `super(condition + (text ? ' - ' + text : ''))`, so any server that attaches a `<text>` produces `message !== condition`. Because the fake can never produce that shape, `wire.conditionOf`'s entire discrimination is graded vacuously, even though three consumers key real behaviour on it: `roomExists` (`condition !== 'item-not-found'` decides whether a read reports an unprobed room), `mamQuery` (`service-unavailable`/`feature-not-implemented` -> the MAM-missing hint) and `configureRoom`'s durability diagnostic.
failure: Delete the whole `.condition` branch — `export const conditionOf = (err: unknown): string => asError(err).message;` — and the suite stays 36 files / 1769 tests GREEN. Against a real Prosody that answers the MAM query `<error><service-unavailable/><text>Archiving is disabled</text></error>`, that same code returns 'service-unavailable - Archiving is disabled', the `===` comparison in mamQuery fails, and the operator gets a raw stanza error instead of the 'enable mod_mam + muc_mam' hint the README promises. Nothing in the suite can see it.
remediation: Make the fixture's `stanzaError` carry a `<text>` the way a real server does — `Object.assign(new Error(`${condition} - ${text}`), { condition, text })` with a default non-empty text — so `message` and `condition` are never interchangeable in any fixture-driven assertion.

Parameterize every condition-driven table (mam-prerequisite.test.ts's `$row.fault`, read-path-creation.test.ts's `$probe`, join-recovery.test.ts's retryable conditions, error-stanza.test.ts's POST_CONDITIONS/JOIN_CONDITIONS) over a `text` axis of ['', 'a server explanation'], driven from ONE shared error builder in fake-xmpp.ts. Add the missing consumer assertion too: read-path-creation must assert that a CONCLUSIVE `item-not-found` (with text) emits NO 'could not establish whether ... exists' stderr line — I verified that after the fixture fix alone the `roomExists` arm is still not discriminated, so the text axis without that assertion leaves half the class open.

summary: `armWaiter`'s `park` is guarded by `if (!settled)` before arming its timeout timer, and `fire` is a no-op once settled — so a waiter that already fired and is then parked arms nothing. Removing the guard keeps the suite green (36 files / 1769 tests), yet it is exactly what stops a leaked long-poll timer: `cancel()` on an already-settled waiter returns before `clearTimeout`. `expectNoLeaks` counts map ENTRIES (pendingJoins/pendingPosts/mamCollectors/waiters) and cannot see a timer at all, so the registry-leak fixture is blind to the timer-leak half of the same class.
failure: With the guard removed: arm a waiter, deliver a live groupchat message so it fires 'message', then call park(60000) and cancel(). `vi.getTimerCount()` is 1, not 0 — a 60 s timer survives a returned fetchRecent and holds the Node event loop open. This is reachable from `blockingMam`: the waiter is armed before `readWindow`, a reflection can fire it during the query's round trip, and `park` is called unconditionally afterwards. I ran this probe against the unmutated source (green, count 0) and the mutated source (red, count 1).
remediation: None needed in src — the guard is correct. Fix the measurement: make `expectNoLeaks` also assert `vi.getTimerCount() === 0` (or take a timer count where fake timers are not in use) so the timer half of 'a finished operation leaves nothing armed' is graded, not just the map half.
testUpgrade: Guard the CLASS 'a finished operation leaves a timer armed'. Extend fake-xmpp.ts's `expectNoLeaks` to include the runtime timer count alongside the four registry sizes, and drive it from a parameterized long-poll teardown table crossing {wake reason: message | timeout | cancel | disconnect} × {park called before the wake, park called after the wake} × {blockMs: 50, 60000}. long-poll-wake.test.ts's 'holds the full budget (and leaks nothing) when nothing is posted' is too narrow: it only exercises the park-then-timeout ordering, which is the one ordering the guard is irrelevant to.

remediationCheck.reliesOn: `armWaiter`'s `fire` closure — `if (settled) return;` at the top and `clearTimeout(timer)` immediately after — which is why an already-settled `cancel()` never clears a timer that `park` armed behind its back.
remediationCheck.newlyRejects: In the suite: any future edit that leaves a timer behind at the end of a long-poll, in any of the ~12 places `expectNoLeaks` is already called.
remediationCheck.testsThatWouldFail: Unknown — I did not run the whole suite with a timer count added to `expectNoLeaks`. Several suites use `vi.useFakeTimers()` and advance them; a call site that returns while a legitimately-still-running timer exists would go red and would need the assertion scoped to after teardown. I am marking this untested for that reason.
remediationCheck.hidesOrFixes: Nothing is broken in src today, so this only closes the measurement gap. If it is skipped, the guard stays correct but unmeasured and the next refactor of `armWaiter` can silently delete it.

summary: `stanzaError` picks the defined condition as the first non-`<text>` element child. Replacing `c.name !== 'text'` with `true` keeps the suite green: the fixture's `errorEl` always emits the condition first and `<text>` second, so the text-first ordering the filter exists for is never produced. This filter is strictly stronger than `@xmpp/error`'s own `fromElement`, which takes the first child element unconditionally — so the plugin is defending against a shape the library does not, with no coverage of the defence.
failure: An error stanza whose children are ordered `<error type='cancel'><text xmlns='urn:ietf:params:xml:ns:xmpp-stanzas'>Room does not exist</text><item-not-found xmlns='...'/></error>` (a presence or message error, which do NOT go through @xmpp/iq). With the guard removed, `condition` becomes 'text', so `RETRYABLE_CONDITIONS.includes('text')` is false — a cold-creation race no longer retries and the join surfaces immediately — and `NOT_AN_OCCUPANT_CONDITIONS.includes('text')` is false, so a bounce that means 'you are not an occupant' no longer triggers re-entry. No test notices.

Add a `childOrder: 'condition-first' | 'text-first'` axis to `errorEl` and cross it into the existing condition tables — error-stanza.test.ts's POST_CONDITIONS and JOIN_CONDITIONS `it.each`, join-recovery.test.ts's retryable-condition rows, and membership-revalidation.test.ts's `occupancyBounceCondition` rows — asserting the same outcome for both orderings. error-stanza.test.ts today is too narrow because every one of its errors comes from the one `errorEl` helper with a single fixed child order.
