summary: `fetchRecent` returns before `blockMs` is ever consulted when `roomExists` is false. seam.ts's blockMs contract says the opposite in as many words: 'Blocking engages whenever the queried window comes back EMPTY, with or without a since: a since-less read of a topic that already has messages returns them at once, but on an empty topic it waits out the budget like any other.' The plugin declares `supportsBlockingFetch: true`, and its README sells block_ms as 'a polling agent's token cost scales with messages, not wall-clock time' and 'XMPP serves this natively'. The conformance blocking case cannot see it because every one of its arms posts to the topic first, so the room always exists.
failure: Against live Prosody: `fetchRecent({ topic: <never-posted topic>, blockMs: 1500 })` returns in 1 ms with `{messages: [], nextCursor: ''}` instead of parking ~1500 ms. The 'native-block-actually-waits' conformance assertion (>= IDLE_BLOCK_FLOOR_MS) never reaches this arm.
remediation: Either honour the budget on the absent-room arm — park on a timer and re-probe `roomExists` at the poll cadence before returning the caller's own cursor — or stop claiming native support for it: state in the README that a topic with no room yet falls back to core's generic long-poll cadence. The second is the smaller, honest change; the first is the one the seam text asks for. Do NOT make the absent-room arm join, which would break 'a read never creates a room'.
testUpgrade: Guard the CLASS 'an arm of fetchRecent that silently drops blockMs'. In packages/conformance/src/cases/blocking.ts add a case that long-polls a topic with NO prior post and asserts the same >= IDLE_BLOCK_FLOOR_MS floor for any backend declaring `supportsBlockingFetch`, so every plugin's absent-topic arm is graded, not just XMPP's. Locally, widen long-poll-wake.test.ts's 'XMPP honours blockMs on every arm of fetchRecent' `$history` axis — which today only carries 'has messages' shapes — with a 'the room does not exist yet' row.

remediationCheck.reliesOn: `roomExists` (rooms.ts:212), whose contract is that only an `<iq type='result'>` is evidence the room is there, and `fetchRecentBlocking` in bridge-core/src/engine/blocking-fetch.ts, which today absorbs this by sleeping `pollIntervalMs` between iterations.
remediationCheck.newlyAccepts: If the park-and-re-probe arm is taken: a long-poll on a topic created by another party mid-wait now returns that party's messages within the budget instead of after core's next poll interval.
remediationCheck.newlyRejects: Nothing, if implemented as park + re-probe. If implemented by joining the room, it would newly CREATE persistent rooms from a read — that is the trap, and it is why the remediation names it as forbidden.
remediationCheck.testsThatWouldFail: read-path-creation.test.ts's 'fetchRecent long-polling' × 'the room does not exist' cells assert both that no room is created AND (in the probe-failure rows) the stderr report; a park-and-re-probe implementation issues MORE disco probes per call, so any of those rows that count sent IQs or assert a single stderr line would need re-derivation. I did not run a candidate implementation, so I have not measured which. Marked untested for that reason.
remediationCheck.hidesOrFixes: Documenting the fallback instead of fixing it leaves the latency (up to `block_poll_interval_ms` extra) but removes the false claim; fixing it removes both. Neither hides anything, because core's wrapper already prevents a hot loop — this is a contract and expectation defect, not an outage.

summary: `disconnect()`'s `this.mamCheck = undefined;` and `this.unprobedRoomsReported.clear();` are unreachable-before-reset: `connect()` already clears both (lines 71-72), and between a disconnect and the next connect nothing can read either — every path to them goes through `this.require()`, which throws while `stopped` is true. Deleting both lines keeps the suite green (36 files / 1769 tests), which is consistent with them being dead rather than merely under-tested.
failure: Not a runtime failure — it is two statements no execution can observe. Mutation evidence: removing them leaves the entire package green against a live server, while removing the CORRESPONDING lines in `connect()` is what a mam-prerequisite or read-path-creation regression would ride on.
remediation: Delete the two lines from `disconnect()`, leaving `connect()` as the single place these two caches are reset. If the symmetry is wanted deliberately, that belongs in the commit message, not the code.
testUpgrade: Guard the CLASS 'per-connection state whose reset lives in both lifecycle halves, so neither is load-bearing'. Add a lifecycle table test that, for each per-connection cache (`mamCheck`, `unprobedRoomsReported`, `identityCollapseReported`, `admittedNick`, `adoptedNick`, `nickAdoption`, `roomNicks`, `rejoins`), asserts through the PUBLIC surface that a connect-disconnect-connect cycle behaves as a fresh plugin — e.g. a MAM-less server on run 1 then a MAM-enabled server on run 2 must serve, and a room whose probe failed on run 1 must report again on run 2. lifecycle-order.test.ts today grades 'exactly one live transport' and not the cache state, so it cannot tell which half of the reset matters.

remediationCheck.reliesOn: `require()` in connection.ts — `if (this.stopped || this.xmpp === undefined) throw` — which is what makes every reader of `mamCheck` (`assertMamAvailable` -> `discoMam` -> `this.require()`) and of `unprobedRoomsReported` (`roomExists` -> `this.require()`) unreachable while disconnected.
remediationCheck.newlyRejects: Nothing.

If the deletion is applied and the reset in `connect()` is ever removed by a later change, the plugin would carry a stale `mamCheck` across a reconnect — which is why the testUpgrade grades the behaviour through connect-disconnect-connect rather than grading which line does the clearing.

summary: `isStreamMissing` accepts a JetStream 503 (`no responders` / JS API unavailable) as "this stream does not exist", and `existingStream` is the only gate `fetchRecent` has. A JetStream API outage — meta-leader election, JS disabled or de-permissioned on the account, a cluster partition — therefore reaches the seam as an empty page with the caller's own cursor replayed, i.e. "this topic is quiet", while the identical fault on the write path throws loudly out of `ensureStream`. The same function's own doc comment says the manager 404s and only the publish 503s, which I confirmed against a real 2.10 server, so no manager path needs the 503 arm at all. Two further conflations ride along: `isMessageMissing` matches `err.code === '404'`, which a real `streams.getMessage` on a MISSING STREAM also returns, and both classifiers fall back to unanchored `/503/` and `/404/` over the message text, so any error string carrying those digits (a port, a byte count, a topic name like `alerts-503`) is misclassified. resource.test.ts's own class comment names exactly this failure ("a branch that reports faults as 'nothing new' turns an auth or permission failure into a bridge that polls forever and says the topic is quiet") but its fault axis injects only at `consumers.get`/`fetch`/`iterate` — never at `streams.info`, which is where the swallow lives.
failure: fetchRecent({topic:'deploys', since:'abc-5', limit:10}) while jsm.streams.info rejects with a NatsError carrying code '503' and message '503' (exactly what the server sends when the JS API has no responder) resolves to {messages: [], nextCursor: 'abc-5'} instead of rejecting. Reproduced: existingStream -> isStreamMissing true -> refuseRivalStream (streams.find also fails, .catch(()=>undefined)) -> returns undefined -> absentTopicPage. With blockMs set it additionally re-polls streams.info every 250ms for the whole budget and still answers 'nothing new'.
remediation: Split the classifier by call surface instead of narrowing one shared predicate. Add `isStreamAbsent(err)` = code '404' AND/OR the phrase `stream not found`, and use it in `streams.ts` `existingStream` and in `read.ts` `fetchRecent`'s catch — both of which only ever see JetStream *manager* errors. Keep the existing 503 arm only in `withStream`, whose `op` for `post` is `js.publish` and genuinely reports a removed stream as 503. Drop the unanchored `/503/` and `/404/` alternations from both message regexes: `reports()` already checks `err.code` structurally, and the phrase alternations still cover the fakes' code-less injections. Give `isMessageMissing` the same treatment so a stream-level 404 is not read as "that sequence holds nothing" in `confirmSequence`.
testUpgrade: Widen resource.test.ts's existing `faults` axis from ['get','fetch','iterate'] to include a `streams.info` injection point in fake-jetstream.ts, and parameterize it over a table of error shapes rather than one message: {code:'404',msg:'stream not found'} (absent -> empty page), {code:'503',msg:'503'} (outage -> reject), {code:'503',msg:'no responders'} (outage -> reject), {code:undefined,msg:'connect ECONNREFUSED 10.0.0.1:5031'} (unrelated -> reject), {code:'404',msg:'no message found'} (message-level). Assert the outcome ('resolved'/'rejected') per row across all three read shapes (no-since, since, blockMs). Add an agreement row in jetstream-agreement.ts for `jsm.streams.getMessage` against a stream that does not exist, so the fake and the real server are both pinned to code 404 / 'stream not found' — that row is what stops the two classifiers drifting apart again. The existing resource.test.ts row 'a stream that vanishes at ${missingOn} mid-read still replays the caller's cursor' is too narrow: it injects only the literal 'stream not found', which is the one shape that should keep swallowing.

remediationCheck.reliesOn: `reports(err, code, wording)` in jetstream.ts:100 — specifically its `(err as {code?: unknown}).code === code` branch, which I verified fires for real errors: a live 2.10 server answers jsm.streams.info/getMessage/consumers.add on a missing stream with code "404" msg "stream not found", and js.publish to a removed stream with code "503" msg "503". Also relies on `withStream` (streams.ts:45) keeping the 503 arm, because that is the only path whose `op` is a publish.
remediationCheck.newlyRejects: fetchRecent during a JetStream API outage (503 / no-responders from streams.info) now rejects instead of resolving to an empty page; a blocking read rejects at once instead of polling out its blockMs.
remediationCheck.testsThatWouldFail: none found — and here is where I looked. resource.test.ts:238 and long-poll.test.ts:137 drive the removal through fake-jetstream's `streamMissingAt`, which throws `new Error('stream not found')` with no code — still matched by the phrase arm. recovery.test.ts and the msg-id post paths use `publishMissing`, whose message is '503 no responders — stream not found' — also matched by the phrase arm, and it is on the `withStream` path which keeps the 503 arm anyway. resource-live.test.ts:448/467/493/529 ('post and fetchRecent still work after ${removal.name}') exercise a real `nats stream rm`, which the server reports as 404 on the manager and 503 on the publish — both still classified correctly under the split. I grepped every call site of isStreamMissing (streams.ts:50, streams.ts:105, read.ts:26) and isMessageMissing (index.ts:63).
remediationCheck.hidesOrFixes: If the split were applied but the unanchored /503/ and /404/ message alternations were left in place, the outage case would still be fixed on the manager path, but an unrelated error whose text carries those digits would still be misread — on the write path a '503'-bearing message would trigger a spurious stream re-provision and republish through withStream, and a '404'-bearing read error inside confirmSequence would still reject a post whose message already landed, telling the caller to send it twice. Both regex arms have to go for the class to close.

summary: The three tests named `${surface} does not describe the cursor and the backendMsgId as different values` are inert on all three of their surfaces. `roleClaim` looks for the `"<noun phrase> as [the] <role>"` shape, and none of README.md, the npm description or src/index.ts is written that way — the npm description says "as BOTH the cursor and the backendMsgId", which the regex's optional `the ` cannot absorb. So `cursorClaim` and `idClaim` are `undefined` on every surface, the `if (... === undefined) return;` on line 267 fires every time, and the assertion below it never executes. The companion test 'the differing-claim check reads a contrast and spares a shared one' proves `roleClaim` works on two synthetic strings, which is precisely why the inertness is invisible: the helper is graded, the surfaces are not. This is the exact shape CLAUDE.md records as the worst of the six architectural-test failure modes — a probe turned tautology that still counts as coverage for the single most load-bearing claim in the package (cursor and backendMsgId are one minted value).
failure: Insert into packages/bridge-nats/README.md the sentence 'The cursor is the bare stream sequence and carries no incarnation;' immediately before the existing backendMsgId paragraph — a flat contradiction of streams.ts `cursorAt`, and the precise misreading the surrounding comment says will make a reader 'write a bare decimal since and be served the newest window instead of resuming'. Reproduced: `vitest run packages/bridge-nats/test/docs.test.ts` reports 166 passed, 0 failed. Independently, evaluating `roleClaim` against the three real surfaces returns undefined/undefined for all six (surface, role) pairs.
remediation: Delete the early-return and make the absence of a claim a failure: assert that `roleClaim(surface.text, 'cursor')` and `roleClaim(surface.text, 'backendMsgId')` are both defined before comparing them, so a surface that stops using the graded phrasing reddens instead of opting out. Then either reword the three surfaces into the `<phrase> as the <role>` shape the probe reads (e.g. npm description: '... an incarnation-qualified stream sequence as the cursor and as the backendMsgId ...'), or replace `roleClaim` with a check that does not depend on one sentence shape — for instance require that every sentence mentioning both roles also mentions 'incarnation', and that no sentence asserts one role has a property the other lacks.
testUpgrade: Guard the class, not this probe: add a meta-test that feeds each doc-extraction helper in docs.test.ts (roleClaim, assertions, proseLines) BOTH a synthetic positive AND the real surfaces, and asserts the helper returns a non-empty result on the real surfaces — a 'the probe finds what it is meant to police' row, which docs.test.ts already has for prose lines and comments but not for roleClaim. Parameterize it over a list of (helper, surface) pairs so a fourth extractor added later is covered by default. Then add a drift table driven from the code: compute the minted value once via `minted()` and assert every surface contains a sentence whose cursor claim and id claim are byte-identical, over a table of negative fixtures (bare-sequence cursor, incarnation-only id, differing shapes) that each must redden.

remediationCheck.reliesOn: `roleClaim` at docs.test.ts:243 and `minted()` at docs.test.ts:218 (which I ran directly and which correctly yields '20260101T000000Z-42' for both cursor and id). Also relies on the sibling test 'README documents the shape in both mapping rows', which already pins the literal `<stream incarnation>-<sequence>` twice in the README and so constrains any rewording.
remediationCheck.newlyRejects: the package's current README, npm description and src/index.ts prose — all three fail the moment the early-return is removed, because none of them carries a roleClaim-shaped sentence. That is the point of the finding, but it means the fix is two changes, not one: the guard AND the prose.
remediationCheck.testsThatWouldFail: 'README.md does not describe the cursor and the backendMsgId as different values', 'the npm description does not describe...', 'src/index.ts does not describe...' — all three go red immediately on removing the early-return, before any prose is rewritten. No other test reads roleClaim; I grepped docs.test.ts for every use.
remediationCheck.hidesOrFixes: Removing the early-return without rewording the surfaces converts three silent no-ops into three red tests, which is the correct intermediate state but is not shippable on its own. If instead only the prose were reworded and the early-return left in, the tests would start asserting for today's wording and go silent again the next time someone rephrases — the guard is the part that must change for the class to close.

summary: The `armIdleClose()` call inside `pull`'s message loop is what makes the idle close measure QUIET rather than TOTAL ELAPSED; without it, `patience.idleMs` becomes a hard deadline for the whole page. Deleting that one line leaves the entire package green at 1715/1715 against a live server. The suite cannot see it because every slow-link case in window.test.ts streams at most 3 records, and idleMs (min(max(200, 3*setupMs), expires)) is always several times the total transfer time in those rows — total and idle are indistinguishable at that size. At page scale the difference is real and reaches the failure `pullPatience`'s own doc warns about: if the first message takes longer than one idle window, the pull closes having read nothing, and pageOrWait mints a cursor at startSeq-1 that never advances.
failure: With `armIdleClose()` removed from the loop: fetchRecent({topic, limit:30}) over a fake link at latencyMs 150 with 30 records returns 6 of 30 messages instead of all 30 (setup ~300ms -> idleMs 900ms, so the pull is cut at 900ms while each message costs 150ms). Reproduced both ways: the same probe passes on the unmutated tree and fails on the mutated one, so the mutation is non-equivalent and the existing suite is simply blind to it.
remediation: No source change — the code is correct today. Close the blind spot in the suite so a future refactor of the patience logic cannot silently reintroduce a total-elapsed deadline.
testUpgrade: Add a parameterized 'the idle close measures quiet, not elapsed' table to window.test.ts, driven over (messageCount, latencyMs) pairs chosen so that messageCount*latencyMs comfortably exceeds pullPatience(2*latencyMs).idleMs — e.g. (30, 150), (60, 100), (10, 400) — asserting the page holds every record and nextCursor is the last one. Include the degenerate row that is the real hazard: a first message delayed past one idle window must still either arrive or leave a cursor strictly above the caller's `since`, never an empty page whose cursor equals what it was handed. The live half already has the instrument for this — test/tcp-proxy.ts takes a `latencyMs` and slow-link-live.test.ts uses it — so add a matching row there over a 30+ message page rather than the current small ones.

remediationCheck.reliesOn: fake-jetstream.ts's per-message `quiet(state.latencyMs)` in the fetch iterator, which charges each delivered record one round trip — that is what makes a steady slow stream expressible without a server. And on `pullPatience` (jetstream.ts:19), whose idleMs derives from setup cost, so the table's rows must be computed from it rather than from a literal.
remediationCheck.newlyRejects: none — no production input changes behaviour; the change is additive test coverage.
remediationCheck.testsThatWouldFail: none found — I ran the proposed 30-message/150ms case against the unmutated tree and it passes in 5.3s. It is slow-ish for a unit file, which is why it belongs as one parameterized table rather than a row per shape.
remediationCheck.hidesOrFixes: Nothing is broken today, so nothing stays broken. If the underlying re-arm were later removed and only this test added, the test catches it; if the test were added but written at the current 3-record scale, it would pass under the removal and would be worse than nothing, because it would look like coverage of the exact invariant it cannot see.

summary: Two pieces of teardown machinery can be deleted with the whole suite staying green, and I traced both to being genuinely redundant rather than merely ungraded. (1) `EphemeralConsumer.reap`'s `await Promise.race([this.adding, delay(DRAIN_TIMEOUT_MS)])`: its doc says a name arriving after teardown 'has nothing left to delete it, and the orphan lingers for inactive_threshold' — but every caller reaps the same `EphemeralConsumer` instance again in its own `finally`/`catch` (pull.ts:83, pull.ts:159, live.ts:68, live.ts:105), and the shared `reaped` flag makes whichever arrives second a no-op. The read's own finally runs as soon as `add` resolves, well before disconnect()'s 2s race expires and nc closes; when `add` takes longer than DRAIN_TIMEOUT_MS, the closer's race times out identically with or without the wait. (2) `blockingFetch`'s `cleanup` promise, `cleanedUp` callback and `polling` flag (pull.ts:110-124): the closer already calls `ephemeral.reap()` itself, so the extra wait for the read's own finally changes only which of the two reaps deletes the consumer. The comments justify both against a design where the closer only closed the batch, which is not the design that shipped. Related: `resource-live.test.ts:263`'s sweep is written for exactly this window ('a closer that reads the consumer's name before the call that mints it deletes nothing') but its offsets are 0/1/2/3/5/10/25/100/400 wall-clock ms against a sub-millisecond localhost round trip, so it never lands inside a `consumers.add`.
failure: Delete the `await Promise.race([this.adding, delay(DRAIN_TIMEOUT_MS)])` line from `reap`: 1715/1715 still pass against a live server. A deterministic probe built to hit the window (fake at latencyMs 200; long-poll started, disconnect() called 300ms in, i.e. inside the add's 200-400ms round trip) also still passes — fake.state.deleted === ['c1'] either way, because blockingFetch's own finally reaps once the name arrives. Same for removing blockingFetch's `if (polling) await Promise.race([cleanup, delay(DRAIN_TIMEOUT_MS)])`.
remediation: Pick one owner for the delete. Either keep the reap in each caller's finally and drop `reap`'s `adding` race plus blockingFetch's `cleanup`/`cleanedUp`/`polling` trio (simplest, and matches what actually runs), or keep the closer as the sole owner and drop the callers' finally reaps. Whichever survives, rewrite the comment to state the risk that is actually live — a consumer whose `add` outlives disconnect()'s DRAIN_TIMEOUT_MS is orphaned for `inactive_threshold` no matter which reaper is used — rather than a risk the other reaper already removes.
testUpgrade: Replace the wall-clock offset sweep in resource-live.test.ts:263 with a table whose window is deterministic instead of hoped-for: drive the same three in-flight shapes (subscribe, fetchRecent, blockMs long-poll) through test/tcp-proxy.ts with `latencyMs` set to 100-200ms so each round trip is measurable, and parameterize the teardown offset in units of that latency (0.25x, 0.5x, 0.75x, 1.5x of a round trip) rather than in raw milliseconds. Assert consumerCount(stream) === 0 for every cell, and add the discriminating row the current sweep is missing: disconnect() landing strictly between `consumers.add` being issued and its reply arriving. That table also grades whichever single reaper survives the simplification, so the class holds after the code shrinks.

remediationCheck.reliesOn: `EphemeralConsumer.reaped` (jetstream.ts:49) making a second reap a no-op, and the four caller-side reaps I enumerated: pull.ts:83 (pull's finally), pull.ts:159 (blockingFetch's finally), live.ts:68 (the loop's catch) and live.ts:105 (after the message loop). Also on session.ts:96's `Promise.race([Promise.all(closing), delay(DRAIN_TIMEOUT_MS)])`, which bounds the closer path identically with or without the inner wait.
remediationCheck.newlyRejects: none — I traced no input whose observable outcome changes, which is exactly why I am filing this as design/KISS rather than as a defect.
remediationCheck.testsThatWouldFail: none found — I ran the full package suite with each removal separately against a live server (1715/1715 both times) and then built a targeted 200ms-latency probe aimed at the window the comment names, which also passed under the removal. I looked at resource-live.test.ts:263 and :379 and :396 and outage.test.ts:164, which are the leak and teardown-budget guards.
remediationCheck.hidesOrFixes: If the simplification is applied and I am wrong about the equivalence, the failure it uncovers is a server-side ephemeral consumer that survives disconnect() for its 30s inactive_threshold — no data loss and self-healing, but it would show up as a rising consumer count under connect/subscribe/disconnect churn. That is precisely what the rewritten latency-driven sweep would catch, which is why the test upgrade should land before or with the simplification, not after.
remediationCheck.interleavings: The orderings I traced, both with two racers on the surviving path: (a) disconnect()'s closer runs while `consumers.add` is in flight — closer's reap returns with name undefined, add resolves, the caller's next await throws on the cleared js/jsm handle, the caller's finally reaps and deletes; (b) `add` resolves first — the caller's finally reaps and deletes, disconnect()'s closer then reaps a no-op via the `reaped` flag; (c) both reach `reap` concurrently — `reaped` is set synchronously before the awaited delete, so only one `consumers.delete` is issued; (d) `add` still pending at DRAIN_TIMEOUT_MS — both racers time out identically and the consumer is orphaned for inactive_threshold, which is the one live risk and is unchanged by the simplification.

summary: Two test oracles carry a comment asserting independence from the code under test, and both are copies of it. `subjectMatches` (fake-jetstream.ts:20) says it is 'implemented here rather than imported from the plugin: this is the rule the fake GRADES the plugin's reads against, and a matcher shared with the code under test agrees with that code's own mistakes' — its nine lines are byte-identical to `captures` in src/naming.ts:27, so it agrees with every mistake `captures` could make. `classify` (jetstream-agreement.ts:31) says it is 'spelled out here so a row cannot inherit the plugin's own mistake' and reuses the same three regex alternations as `isStreamMissing`/`isMessageMissing`. For `captures` the risk is mitigated elsewhere — config.test.ts:1030 grades it against a genuinely independent regex oracle over 2000 generated pairs, with an emission check — but nothing plays that role for the classifiers, and `classify` and the plugin already disagree on a real error: a live `jsm.streams.getMessage` against a missing stream returns code '404' with message 'stream not found', which `classify` calls 'stream-missing' (message checked first, code ignored) and `isMessageMissing` calls true (code checked first). No agreement row covers that call, so the divergence is invisible.
failure: Any error in `captures` — say treating a trailing '>' as matching zero tokens — is reproduced identically by the fake, so every window.test.ts row that depends on subject filtering agrees with the bug; only config.test.ts's separate regex oracle would redden. And `classify(err)` vs `isMessageMissing(err)` return different classifications today for the concrete error a real 2.10 server sends for getMessage on a missing stream (code '404', message 'stream not found'), with no row exercising it.
remediation: Make the fake import `captures` from src/naming.ts and delete `subjectMatches` — the duplicate buys nothing that config.test.ts's regex oracle does not already buy, and its comment currently makes a false promise about where the independence lives. For `classify`, either derive it from the plugin's own predicates and rename it to say so, or make it genuinely independent by keying on `err.code` alone (404/503) with no message matching, so a row disagreeing with the plugin's message-text arms is a red test.
testUpgrade: Add a table to jetstream-agreement.ts that pins the (code, message) pair the real server returns for each failure the plugin classifies — getMessage on a missing sequence, getMessage on a missing stream, streams.info on a missing stream, consumers.add on a missing stream, publish to a removed stream, streams.add on a name in use, streams.add with overlapping subjects — and assert, per row, both the server's shape AND the plugin's own `isStreamMissing`/`isMessageMissing` verdict on it. That makes the classifiers graded against the server rather than against a sibling copy of themselves, and a new failure shape arrives with no row and fails by default, the way the existing `covers`/primitive completeness gate already works for the fake's surface.

remediationCheck.reliesOn: config.test.ts:1030's `oracle` (a regex-based NATS interest matcher) and its emission check at :1038, which together are what actually grade `captures` — that is the branch I depend on to say deleting `subjectMatches` loses no coverage. And on the live probe showing jsm.streams.getMessage on a missing stream returns code '404' / 'stream not found'.
remediationCheck.newlyRejects: none in production code; in tests, a `classify` keyed on err.code alone would reject the fake's code-less injected errors, so the fake would have to attach codes to the errors it throws.
remediationCheck.testsThatWouldFail: none found — I checked that window.test.ts's fake-side rows and jetstream-agreement-live.test.ts grade the same `expected` literals, so swapping subjectMatches for an import changes no expectation. Making `classify` code-only WOULD break every fake-side agreement row that throws a bare `new Error('stream not found')` (fake-jetstream.ts streamMissingAt, addFails, getMessageMissing, publishMissing) until those errors carry codes — that is the real cost of the second half of this remediation and it should be done together with the code-attachment, not before.
remediationCheck.hidesOrFixes: If only the comments were corrected and the duplication left, the classifiers stay ungraded against the server and finding 1's class can recur under a new spelling. If only `subjectMatches` were deduplicated, the more consequential half — the classifier divergence — is untouched.

summary: The CLI section's justification sentence is ungrammatical and reads as a botched template substitution: 'since that default names a different deployment's another cluster, stream prefix, handle and topic allowlist.' Because the entry sits at or above the caller's cursor, every later catch-up throws on it again: the topic is wedged. The module treats `messages` as `unknown` precisely because an `ok:true` body is not a contract, and the README states the plugin never assumes it got what it asked for — so this input is inside the package's own stated threat model.

At t+300 ms the retired dial rejects; ensureSocket's `attempt.catch` correctly returns on the session mismatch, but reconnect()'s catch then sees `dialCooldownUntil (0) <= Date.now()` and calls backOffDialling() -> session 1 now has dialCooldownUntil = now + 500 and dialBackoffMs = 1000. summary: A `<store_path>.lock.break` left behind by a bridge killed inside `StoreLock.replaceStale` permanently disables the automatic stale-claim take-over. `replaceStale` opens the break sibling with `flag: 'wx'` and returns `false` on ANY failure, including EEXIST -- it never asks whether the process the leftover names is still alive, and nothing ever removes it. Every subsequent start then reports the store as claimed by a process that is long gone, so the crashed-bridge recovery the class doc and the README promise is exactly the thing that stops working after a crash. The diagnostic names only `.lock`, never `.lock.break`, so an operator who removes `.lock` gets one successful start and is back in the same state at the next crash -- forever.
failure: Given /tmp/s/store.jsonl.lock containing a dead pid and /tmp/s/store.jsonl.lock.break containing anything (the state a SIGKILL between the `wx` create and the `renameSync` leaves), `new StoreLock(path).claim()` throws "ObservedStore: '/tmp/s/store.jsonl' is already claimed by process 637268 through '/tmp/s/store.jsonl.lock' ... If no such process is running, remove '/tmp/s/store.jsonl.lock'." on attempt 1, 2 and 3 (reproduced), and store.jsonl.lock.break is still present afterwards. Expected: the take-over replaces a claim whose process is gone. Actual: connect() fails permanently and names the wrong file.
remediation: In `replaceStale`, on an EEXIST from the break-file create, read the pid out of the leftover with the existing `lockHolder(this.breakPath)`; if -- and only if -- it returns a DEFINITE pid that `processExists` says is dead, `unlinkSync` the leftover and retry the `wx` create exactly once, giving up if the retry also EEXISTs. Treat an unreadable/empty break file as ALIVE and do not unlink it, so that the create-then-write window in which a competitor's fresh break file is momentarily empty cannot be mistaken for a corpse. Separately, name `${this.path}.break` alongside `${this.path}` in the claim-refused message so the manual remedy is complete.
testUpgrade: Parameterize a table over the CLASS "a leftover sibling of the claim protocol must not outlive the process that made it": rows = each path in siblingPaths() (lock, break, mark, tmp) x leftover content (a live pid, a dead pid, empty, garbage), asserting that a fresh StoreLock(path).claim() succeeds whenever no live process is named and fails otherwise. Deriving the rows from siblingPaths() rather than hard-coding .lock.break means a sibling a later change adds is covered the moment it lands. test/store-lock-race.test.ts is too narrow to have caught this: its 12 boundaries all run BOTH claimants to completion inside one process, so a break file is always consumed by the rename or the finally-unlink and the leaked-leftover state is never constructed.

remediationCheck.reliesOn: `lockHolder(path)` (store-file.ts:175) -- `Number.isInteger(pid) && pid > 0 ? pid : undefined`, i.e. it already returns undefined for an empty or garbled file, which is the exact branch the fix depends on to refuse to unlink a competitor's half-written break file; and `processExists(pid)` (store-file.ts:181), whose `return (err as NodeJS.ErrnoException).code === 'EPERM'` branch keeps a process we may not signal counted as ALIVE.
remediationCheck.newlyAccepts: A start against store.jsonl.lock naming a dead pid AND a leftover store.jsonl.lock.break naming a dead pid -- today a permanent hard failure, after the fix a successful take-over.
remediationCheck.newlyRejects: Nothing new is rejected. The added arm only runs on the EEXIST path that already returned false, and it still returns false when the leftover names a live process or carries no readable pid.
remediationCheck.testsThatWouldFail: none found -- I ran the 12 store-lock-race.test.ts boundaries and the store-single-writer.test.ts PHASES/FOREIGN_CLAIMS tables mentally against the new arm: none of them ever leaves a break file behind, so the arm is unreachable in every existing row. I did not execute the patched code, so this is a reading of those two files, not a measurement.
remediationCheck.hidesOrFixes: If applied while the leak itself remains, the leak is still there -- a killed take-over still orphans a break file -- but it is now self-healing on the next start instead of terminal. What stays broken: the claim-refused message still names only .lock unless the second half of the remediation is applied too, and a squatter who can write the store's directory can still park a break file naming a LIVE pid of their own and block take-over indefinitely (the README's "keep it in a directory only this account can write" is the only defence there).
remediationCheck.interleavings: (1) A killed mid-take-over, B starts later: B reads A's pid from the break file, A is dead, B unlinks and re-creates, B proceeds -- one holder. (2) A and B both start on the same stale claim: A wins the wx create; B's create EEXISTs, B reads A's LIVE pid, processExists true, B does not unlink and returns false -- one holder, unchanged from today. (3) The dangerous ordering -- B's read lands inside A's create-then-write window and sees an empty file: lockHolder returns undefined, the fix treats that as alive and does NOT unlink, so B cannot drop A's fresh break file. This is why the fix must not fold undefined into "dead". (4) Two starters both reading the same DEAD leftover pid: both unlink, both attempt wx, exactly one create wins; the loser returns false. The renameSync-based publish onto .lock is untouched, so the two-holders hazard the original design closed stays closed.

summary: Resolving a topic marks its chat as served (index.ts:130 -> chats.ts:33 -> store.serve), and serve() appends a `#served [...]` line to the observed-message store file and adds the id to an in-memory Set that nothing ever bounds. A plain fetchRecent is enough to trigger it, so a READ is a durable write. Two consequences: the store file grows monotonically from read traffic with no reclamation path -- compactIfDue is armed only by record eviction (evictedSinceRewrite >= max(maxPerChat, size())), so on a store with no record churn compaction never runs and the lines never leave -- and every one of those chats becomes permanently exempt from observed_max_chats (admit returns true for any served chat and evictLeastRecentUnserved skips them), so the cap the README sells as the bound on anyone-can-add-the-bot traffic stops bounding anything. Topic strings reach fetchRecent through core's POST/FETCH allowlist, which includes post_topics regex patterns -- a supported configuration under which the topic space is model-chosen, not operator-sized.
failure: Connect with observed_max_chats: 1, then issue 500 read-only fetchRecent({topic}) calls on 500 distinct numeric topics. Reproduced: the store file contains served-lines=500 bytes=12024 records=0 -- 500 bookkeeping lines and zero messages -- and all 500 chats are now cap-exempt, so applyChatCap's `while (byChat.size > maxChats && evictLeastRecentUnserved())` can evict none of them once traffic arrives. Expected: a read does not durably grow the store, and observed_max_chats continues to bound unserved chats.
remediation: Bound the served set the way the file is already bounded: cap ObservedStore.served at SERVED_ID_MEMORY with the same newest-last eviction rememberEvicted uses, so memory and file agree, and arm compactIfDue on bookkeeping lines as well as on evicted records (count serve()'s appends into a counter the compaction threshold reads) so a quiet store still reclaims. Separately, decide deliberately whether a read should serve at all: making serve() a post/subscribe-only effect, with fetchRecent resolving through chatIdFor without the mark, removes the read-is-a-write surprise entirely and leaves chat_map as the operator-sized protection the README already tells people to use.
testUpgrade: A parameterized case over the CLASS "a seam call on an unbounded, caller-chosen topic space must not grow unbounded durable state": rows = each seam method (fetchRecent, post, subscribe, resolveIdentity) x N in {1, 200, 2000} distinct fresh topics, asserting that store-file bytes and the served-mark count stay under a fixed ceiling and that observed_max_chats still evicts after the sweep. Widen docs.test.ts's existing chat-cap cases the same way -- they use a 6-chat flood and 2 named ops chats, so no row in the suite ever names more topics than the cap, which is why the cap's own defeat is invisible today.

remediationCheck.reliesOn: `rememberEvicted` (store.ts:352) -- its `for (const oldest of this.evicted) { if (size <= LIMIT) break; delete }` newest-last trim over a Set is the exact mechanism the served cap would reuse; and journalText's existing `[...this.served].slice(-SERVED_ID_MEMORY)` (store.ts:396), which already assumes the newest 1000 marks are the ones worth keeping.
remediationCheck.newlyAccepts: A store that has been asked about more than SERVED_ID_MEMORY distinct chats -- today that keeps every one cap-exempt forever; after the fix the oldest marks age out and those chats become evictable again.
remediationCheck.newlyRejects: Nothing is rejected at the seam. The behavioural loss is real though: the 1001st-oldest served chat loses its never-evict protection, which is history the Bot API cannot backfill. That is already the file's behaviour across a restart, so the fix makes memory agree with disk rather than introducing a new loss.
remediationCheck.testsThatWouldFail: none found -- I checked store.test.ts's SERVED_PERSISTENCE_CASES, SERVED_MARK_CASES and 'bounds the served marks a compaction carries however many chats were named', plus docs.test.ts's three chat-cap cases and unconfigured-chat-ingest.test.ts's STARVATION_CELLS. None names more than a handful of chats, so a 1000-entry cap is above every row. The second half of the remediation (stop serving on a read) WOULD break docs.test.ts 'keeps a chat a seam call only read, across the rewrite that compacts the store file', which asserts precisely that a read protects a chat -- that test is the codification of the behaviour, so changing it is a deliberate contract change, not an incidental break.
remediationCheck.hidesOrFixes: Capping the set alone fixes the memory half and leaves the file half broken: a quiet store still accumulates #served lines with no compaction to reclaim them, because the threshold is still record-driven. Arming compaction on bookkeeping lines is the part that actually stops the file growing. Neither half addresses the design question of whether a read should be a write -- if that is left as is, the surprise remains and only its cost is bounded.

summary: StoreFile.note() is documented as 'Write one bookkeeping line, reporting rather than throwing when it cannot be written', but it only reports when appendFileSync THROWS. write() (line 370-372) returns silently when openFd() yields no descriptor -- the file was closed on purpose, or a reopen failed on EMFILE/EACCES/ENOSPC -- so note()'s catch never fires and nothing is reported. The line that goes missing on that branch is ObservedStore.serve's #served mark, i.e. exactly the persisted chat-cap protection the README promises survives a restart ('That protection is written into the store file, so a chat a seam call named in one run is still protected at the next load'). The chat stays protected for the life of the process and silently loses that protection at the next load, with no stderr line anywhere.
failure: With the append descriptor unavailable (the store file's directory made unwritable after open(), so openFd()'s openAppend() throws and returns undefined), a seam call naming a fresh topic runs serve(chatId) -> file.note('#served ["-100..."]') -> write() returns at `if (fd === undefined) return;`. Output: no exception, no diagnostic, served holds the id in memory only. After a restart under a chat flood the chat is evicted and its history -- which the Bot API has no endpoint to backfill -- is gone.
remediation: Give write() a way to say it wrote nothing (return a boolean, or split out a tryWrite) and have note() report on that branch with the same 'bookkeeping-line' kind it already uses, e.g. `could not record '#served' in <path> (no append descriptor) - this run is unaffected and the next restart loses what the line carried`. ObservedStore.append already asks file.writable() first so its own contract is unchanged.

Today only the write-throws column exists, and only for the store's record path -- store-torn-write.test.ts's CELLS drive appendFileSync failures, never the no-descriptor branch, so half the table has never been executed.

summary: Waiters.wake's `if (seq > w.sinceSeq)` can never be false. wake has exactly one caller -- TelegramPlugin.ingest (index.ts:402) -- which passes a freshly stamped rec.seq, and park is only ever reached with a sinceSeq that requireOwnCursor has already held at or below store.highWater(). Since rec.seq = this.nextSeq++ and highWater() === nextSeq - 1, every woken seq is strictly greater than every parked sinceSeq by construction. The class doc sells the condition as load-bearing ('only a seq above sinceSeq may [unpark it]'), which reads as a real filter a reviewer must reason about.
failure: Mutating `seq > w.sinceSeq` to `seq >= w.sinceSeq` (verified applied by diff) leaves all 722 tests green -- including the conformance blocking cases and guarantees.test.ts's WAKEUP_CELLS. No input reaches the false arm, so the branch is graded by nothing and a future change that made it reachable would land unprotected.
remediation: Either drop the comparison and wake every waiter on the chat -- the parked call re-queries anyway, and wakeAll's own doc explicitly states that returning early/empty is always safe -- or keep it and make it an assertion whose violation is loud, so a future second caller of wake that broke the invariant fails rather than silently losing a wakeup. summary: The invariant 'a credential sent to a NON-loopback host over an unencrypted transport must warn the operator' is implemented eight times, once per backend, and is absent from the ninth networked backend. Matrix (config.ts:198), Discord (creds.ts:26), NATS (config.ts:230), Redis (diagnostics.ts:93), Telegram (diagnostics.ts:41), Zulip (index.ts:58), Slack (config.ts:247 and socket.ts:95) and XMPP (config.ts:88) each classify via net-util's `plaintextRemoteOrigin`/`isLoopbackHost`. `grep -rn 'ssl|sslmode|plaintext|loopback|127\.0\.0\.1' packages/bridge-postgres/src/*.ts` returns exactly one line: `DEFAULT_URL = 'postgres://parley:parley@127.0.0.1:5432/parley'`. There is no central test of the class — each of the eight is graded only by its own package's creds-warning.test.ts (five files, 703 lines, five different fixture idioms), so the package that never implemented it is invisible to every package-scoped reader. This is the exact shape packages/conformance/test/backend-config-keys.test.ts:6 was written for ('six backends refused an unknown backend_config key and four accepted one in silence, and nothing in the repo graded the difference') — the remedy pattern exists and this invariant did not get it.
failure: Input: `backend_config: { url: 'postgres://parley:hunter2@db.example.com:5432/parley' }` with no `sslmode` — a plain TCP DSN to a remote host. Output: bridge-postgres connects and emits nothing about the password crossing the network in the clear. The identical shape on any of the other eight (`site_url: 'http://zulip.example.com'`, `homeserver_url: 'http://matrix.example.com'`, `api_url: 'http://slack.example.com'`) produces a named stderr warning naming the key and the origin. `node-postgres` defaults `ssl` to false, so the DSN above authenticates over cleartext unless the server refuses it. No test anywhere fails.
remediation: Two parts, and the second is the finding. (a) Have bridge-postgres classify its DSN host with net-util's `isLoopbackHost` (which it can already reach — @sharptrick/parley-net-util is in its `dependencies` and src/listener.ts:1 already imports from it) and warn when the DSN carries a password to a non-loopback host with no `sslmode`/`ssl` in force. (b) Move the invariant to one place: a repo-scope case in packages/conformance/test that, for every package exporting a seam constructor, connects with a remote-host credential-carrying config and asserts a warning names the offending key and the origin — modelled on backend-config-keys.test.ts, which already derives the backend set from the seam and the probed keys from each plugin's own refusal message.
testUpgrade: CLASS = 'a security predicate every backend implements for itself, so the backend that implements none is invisible'. The guard must be one `it.each` whose rows are derived from the seam (a package is graded iff its export's prototype carries connect/disconnect/subscribe/post/fetchRecent/resolveIdentity), never from a list of backend names — so bridge-postgres and the eleventh backend are rows by construction. Cross it with a host axis (loopback literal, `localhost`, a registrable name shaped like a loopback address such as `127.0.0.1.example.com`, a remote name) and a scheme axis, and assert 'warns' or 'does not warn' per cell; the five per-package creds-warning.test.ts files are then collapsible into per-backend row data rather than five hand-written fixtures. That also picks up the drift I measured in the warning SINK (five backends use console.warn, four use process.stderr.write) as a single row assertion instead of nine independent conventions.

remediationCheck.reliesOn: packages/conformance/test/backend-config-keys.test.ts's `isPluginConstructor`/`workspaceManifests` derivation, reused verbatim; and net-util's `isLoopbackHost`, whose contract ('an unproven host is warned about rather than excused', timing/plaintext.ts:36) is the fail direction the new postgres call must adopt.

summary: `this.connecting` exists so that `tearDown` never calls `disconnect()` on a reader whose handshake is still in flight — index.ts:66-73 spells out the consequence: node-redis assigns the socket only once the TCP connect resolves, so a `disconnect()` before that flips the client closed with no socket to destroy, the handshake then completes onto a live socket, and every later `disconnect()` throws `ClientClosedError` on an orphan nothing can close. But `connectReader`'s `finally` deletes the reader from `connecting` as soon as `withDeadline` SETTLES, and `withDeadline` can settle by its own timer while `reader.connect()` is still pending. Both callers then run `retireReader(reader)` -> `reader.disconnect()` — the exact action the set exists to prevent, reached through a different door.
failure: A reader whose TCP connect has not yet resolved when `withDeadline(connectTimeoutMs)` fires — e.g. `subscribe()` or a blocking `fetchRecent` opened against an endpoint that starts completing its TCP handshake at roughly `connect_timeout_ms`. `blockingRead`'s finally / `startReadLoop`'s catch calls `retireReader`, which disconnects a client with no socket; if the TCP connect then lands, the socket is live, unreferenced and unclosable, and every later `disconnect()` on it throws. I could not force the window open: the reader's socket-level `connectTimeout` is the SAME `connectTimeoutMs`, and the pre-handshake `reconnectStrategy` also rejects, so the two watchdogs almost always fire together — which is why I am marking this PLAUSIBLE rather than confirmed.
remediation: Do not remove the reader from `connecting` on the deadline path. Keep it in the set (and let the underlying `reader.connect()` promise own the eventual close) until `reader.connect()` itself settles: e.g. `void work.finally(() => this.connecting.delete(reader))` on the raw connect promise, with `retireReader` skipping any reader still in `connecting` exactly as `tearDown` does, and the raw promise's own continuation doing the disconnect.
testUpgrade: The class is 'a reader is closed while node-redis has not yet assigned it a socket'. live-connections.test.ts's `failingReaders` rows are the existing tests too narrow to catch it: `proxy.stallNewConnections()` ACCEPTS TCP and then goes silent, so node-redis always holds the socket by the time the deadline fires — the pre-socket window is structurally unreachable there. Add a WHERE-THE-HANDSHAKE-DIES axis to those rows: {TCP never completes (blackholed ip), TCP completes exactly at the deadline (a proxy that accepts after connect_timeout_ms), TCP completes then silence (today's stall)} × {subscribe, one blocking fetch, three blocking fetches}, asserting `proxy.live() === 0` and no `TCPSocketWrap` growth after each, and additionally that no `ClientClosedError` escapes.

remediationCheck.reliesOn: index.ts:123-128 `tearDown`'s `if (this.connecting.has(reader)) continue;` — I mutation-tested that branch (removed it) and live-connections.test.ts:394 'connect·(disconnect ∥ subscribe) returns every socket' went RED, so the branch is real and graded. The fix depends on `retireReader` gaining the same exclusion.
remediationCheck.newlyAccepts: A reader whose deadline fired but whose connect later succeeds is now closed by the connect's own continuation rather than left to `retireReader` — i.e. a close that today happens too early happens later instead.
remediationCheck.newlyRejects: none at the seam. `subscribe()` and the long poll still reject/return `[]` on the deadline exactly as now; only the disposal of the losing socket moves.
remediationCheck.testsThatWouldFail: I did not run this fix, so I cannot name any with confidence. The ones most at risk are the ones that assert prompt disposal rather than eventual disposal: subscribe-hardening.test.ts:519 'a superseded reader serves nobody' asserts `reader.disconnect` toHaveBeenCalled and `readers` empty immediately after `await run`, and failure-modes.test.ts:644 reads the handle table once rather than polling. If disposal moves onto a continuation of the raw connect promise, either could observe the reader one tick early. Untested.
remediationCheck.hidesOrFixes: If the underlying node-redis behaviour is not what index.ts:66-73 claims, this fix hides nothing and costs nothing — it just defers a close. If the claim is right, it closes the orphan; it does NOT close the same window in `openCommandClient` (client.ts:121-123), which disconnects the command client on the identical deadline path and would still orphan it.
remediationCheck.interleavings: Three orderings matter. (i) deadline fires, connect still pending, connect later succeeds — today: disconnect on a socketless client, then a live orphan; with the fix: the connect continuation closes it. (ii) deadline fires, connect later rejects — with the fix the continuation must tolerate a client that never opened, i.e. `.catch(() => undefined)` on the close. (iii) two callers on the new path: a `subscribe` and a `blockingRead` each hold their own reader and their own entry in `connecting`, and a `tearDown` between them must still skip both and leave each one's continuation to close it — this is the interleaving I did not exercise, and the reason this fix is untested.

summary: The guard that claims to check 'every interpolation of every page it renders, reachable or not' only scans template literals matching /<!doctype|<\/[a-z]+>/i. A template that opens a tag and closes it in a different literal — the shape every row/partial helper takes — is invisible to it, so an unescaped attribute interpolation ships with the suite green.
remediation: In the `pages` builder, replace the `/<!doctype|<\/[a-z]+>/i` document filter with: keep any template literal that contains a `<` AND at least one `${...}` interpolation. That is the property the guard is actually about (markup carrying interpolated data), and it does not depend on the literal being a whole document.
testUpgrade: The class is 'an architectural guard whose subject list is derived by a heuristic that a legal refactor can fall outside of'. Guard it two ways at once: (1) widen the selector as above, and (2) add a self-test alongside it, in the shape hygiene.test.ts already uses for its skip rule — a SYNTHETIC table of source snippets with an `offends` column, including a partial-tag row (`` `<li title="${x}">` ``), a whole-document row, a concatenated-render row, and a non-markup template row, asserting the selector reaches both verdicts. Without (2) the widened selector is itself a rule nobody has watched fail. Existing test too narrow: 'the auth layer escapes at every interpolation of every page it renders, reachable or not' — its `it('finds the interpolations to check')` floor only asserts >= 5 interpolations, which the three current whole-document literals already satisfy, so a new unscanned page never lowers it.

remediationCheck.reliesOn: The same `readdirSync(DIR)` + `[...source.matchAll(/`(?:[^`\\]|\\.)*`/g)]` scan already in the test; only the `.filter((t) => /<!doctype|<\/[a-z]+>/i.test(t))` predicate changes. It also relies on the existing `bound` map from `/const (\w+) = (.+);$/gm` to resolve a name to its escaping definition.
remediationCheck.newlyAccepts: none — the widened predicate is a strict superset of the current one for literals carrying interpolations
remediationCheck.newlyRejects: Any template literal in a non-test auth source that contains a `<` and an interpolation that does not pass through escapeHtml. I enumerated every such literal in the 13 sources: only three exist (the consent page, the refusal page, and the refusal body), all already scanned and all already escaped. The five other `<`-bearing literals (invariants.ts `/mcp<anything>`, oidc-discovery.ts `<issuer>/...` and `/realms/<realm>/...`, owner.ts `scrypt$N=..$<saltB64>$<hashB64>`, remote-auth.ts `Record<keyof RemoteAuthOptions, …>`) are inside JSDoc and carry no `${}`, so the interpolation condition excludes them.
remediationCheck.testsThatWouldFail: none found — I enumerated every template literal in every non-test file under src/auth with a script and confirmed the widened rule changes no verdict on the current tree; and the widened rule still fails the 'consent-page.ts: ${consentId} is escaped' row when consent_id escaping is removed, which I verified as a killed mutation.
remediationCheck.hidesOrFixes: If applied while a partial-template render function already exists with an unescaped interpolation, the guard turns red and the escape must be added — it fixes the blind spot rather than hiding it. What stays broken is that the guard remains a source-regex: a page rendered from outside src/auth, or one built with String concatenation and no template literal at all, is still unseen.

Flipping it to `>` leaves the suite green and puts it out of step with the sweeper's `expiresAtMs < nowMs`, which keeps the same record.
failure: Mutate eviction.ts line 34 to `state.expiresAtMs > nowMs`. Ran the auth + transport + stated-bounds + config suites: 1898/1898 passed. Under that mutation a client whose only credential expires at exactly `now` is classified as holding nothing and becomes a first-pass eviction candidate, while ParleyOAuthProvider.sweep and challengeForAuthorizationCode both still treat that record as live — the registration is evicted out from under a credential the rest of the provider will still honour for one tick.
remediation: Add an eviction-liveness row to packages/bridge-core/src/stated-bounds.test.ts as a StatedBound with `legal: 'at-or-above'` and `bound: nowMs`, probing evictionCandidate directly at expiresAtMs = nowMs - 1, nowMs and nowMs + 1 with a single client state, and asserting the equality tick counts as live.

Generalise the stated-bounds table to carry the auth layer's four time comparisons as rows — evictionCandidate's `>=`, sweep's `<` on codes/redeeming/refresh/pending, sweep's `<` on access (seconds, not ms), and verifyAccessToken's `expiresAt < now/1000` — each probed at bound-1, bound, bound+1 and each asserting the same verdict at the equality tick. That widened generator also catches a unit mismatch (the access map is in seconds and the rest in milliseconds), which no current row would notice. Existing test too narrow: 'a client whose ... has expired becomes evictable again' drives an expiry far in the past, so it cannot see the boundary move by one.

remediationCheck.reliesOn: stated-bounds.test.ts's existing `StatedBound` interface and its three-cell (bound-1, bound, bound+1) driver; and on evictionCandidate being directly importable from ./auth/eviction.js, which stated-bounds.test.ts already does for MAX_CLIENTS/MAX_PENDING/shedCrowdedest.

summary: 'every 401 this server emits carries the same error message' is false: the SDK's requireBearerAuth answers a missing Authorization header with error_description="Missing Authorization header" and a non-Bearer scheme with "Invalid Authorization header format, expected 'Bearer TOKEN'", both before OidcTokenVerifier runs. The test that names this sentence as the property it grades builds its table only from token-content defects, so it cannot fail on the two shapes that falsify it.
failure: Against a booted OIDC front door: `POST /mcp` with no Authorization header returns 401 with `WWW-Authenticate: Bearer error="invalid_token", error_description="Missing Authorization header"`, while `POST /mcp` with `Authorization: Bearer <token signed by a rogue key>` returns 401 with `error_description="invalid or expired access token"`. Two distinguishable 401 surfaces; the doc says there is one. Traced through node_modules/@modelcontextprotocol/sdk/dist/esm/server/auth/middleware/bearerAuth.js lines 13-19 and the REJECTIONS table at packages/bridge-core/src/auth/oidc-remote.test.ts:398-408, every row of which mints or names a token.
remediation: Narrow the doc sentence to what the code delivers and what actually matters: 'every 401 this server emits about a PRESENTED TOKEN carries the same error message — an unauthorized caller who holds a token learns nothing about which check failed. A request with no Authorization header, or one that is not a Bearer credential, is answered by the SDK's own pre-verification 401 and is distinguishable, which reveals nothing the caller did not already know.'
testUpgrade: The class is 'a doc sentence quantified over a set larger than the generator that grades it'. Extend the REJECTIONS generator in oidc-remote.test.ts to two labelled partitions rather than one list: a TOKEN_REJECTIONS partition (today's rows) asserted to collapse to exactly one surface, and a PRE_TOKEN_REJECTIONS partition (no header, `Authorization: Basic x`, `Authorization: Bearer` with no token, a lower-case `bearer` scheme) asserted only to be 401 and to leak no gate wording — plus an assertion that the doc paragraph's quantifier matches the partition the suite actually collapses. That last assertion is what stops the sentence and the table drifting apart again. Existing test too narrow: 'emits one and only one response surface across every rejection reason' says 'every rejection reason' in its own name while enumerating only token-content reasons.

remediationCheck.reliesOn: The SDK's bearerAuth catch block, which routes InvalidTokenError to `res.set('WWW-Authenticate', buildWwwAuthHeader(error.errorCode, error.message))` — the branch that echoes the message verbatim. Both pre-verifier throws are InvalidTokenError, so they take the same branch and differ only in text.
remediationCheck.newlyAccepts: none — doc + test change, no production behaviour moves
remediationCheck.newlyRejects: none
remediationCheck.testsThatWouldFail: none found — the existing 'emits one and only one response surface' row keeps passing verbatim because the new partition is asserted separately. I checked hygiene.test.ts's 'no doc describes an e2e gate the suite does not implement' rule: it only fires on paragraphs that name an *.e2e.test.ts path and mention a skip, so editing this Security-notes paragraph does not trip it.

Fixing the sentence is the load-bearing half; the test partition only stops it drifting again. Making the claim literally true instead — swallowing the SDK's pre-verifier messages — would mean wrapping requireBearerAuth and rewriting its WWW-Authenticate, which breaks the SDK's documented error contract for no security gain.

summary: isAccessToken's last line accepts any token that stamps no `typ` and carries no nonce/at_hash/c_hash. That is a deliberate, tested decision, but it means the ID-token defence is inert for every IdP that does not stamp `typ` — and docs/keycloak-integration.md, which says 'any spec-compliant IdP works', never warns against the one config that turns it into a vulnerability: setting auth.oidc.audience to the connector's client_id.
failure: Configure auth.oidc against a typ-less IdP (Auth0/Okta/Azure-style: JOSE header {alg, kid} with no typ, no `typ` claim) with `audience: "<connector client_id>"` and `allowed_subjects: ["<user sub>"]`. Present that user's ID token from the authorization-code flow — which per OIDC Core 3.1.3.6 need carry neither `nonce` (code flow) nor `at_hash` (OPTIONAL from the token endpoint) — as `Authorization: Bearer <id_token>`. isAccessToken returns true (declared = [], both `some` calls false, ID_TOKEN_ONLY_CLAIMS.every(...) true), aud matches, the subject gate passes, and the caller gets 200 and full MCP tool access from a login receipt. The repo already names this shape: packages/bridge-core/src/auth/keycloak.e2e.test.ts:260 calls audience==client_id 'exactly the vulnerable shape', but that test's defence is Keycloak's `typ: ID` claim, which a typ-less IdP does not emit.
remediation: Two parts. (1) In docs/keycloak-integration.md's config reference, next to `audience:`, state plainly: never set this to your connector's client_id — an ID token's `aud` IS the client_id, and for an IdP that does not stamp `typ` on its tokens that makes a login receipt indistinguishable from an access token; use a dedicated audience string or the canonical resource URL. (2) Add an opt-in `auth.oidc.require_typed_access_token: true` that makes ACCESS_TOKEN_TYPES membership mandatory rather than merely decisive, for operators on an IdP that does stamp RFC 9068 `at+jwt`.
testUpgrade: The class is 'a claim-shape heuristic whose defence is inert for a whole family of IdPs, with the residual visible only in a test comment'. Parameterize the KIND_MATRIX in oidc-token-kinds.test.ts over an ISSUER_STYLE axis — {stamps typ in the claim (Keycloak), stamps typ in the JOSE header only, stamps no typ at all} — crossed with the existing (nonce, at_hash, c_hash) shapes, and add an AUDIENCE axis {resource URL, dedicated string, the azp value}. The row (no typ, no id-only claims, aud === azp) is the one this finding is about; make it explicit and label it accepted-with-require_typed_access_token-off / refused-with-it-on, so the residual is a graded cell rather than a paragraph. Existing test too narrow: KIND_MATRIX's ['neither nonce nor at_hash', {}, [true, ...]] records the acceptance but says nothing about the audience configuration that makes it reachable.

remediationCheck.reliesOn: isAccessToken's existing three-step structure (deny-list, allow-list, claim-shape fallback) and ACCEPTED/NON_ACCESS_TOKEN_TYPES; the opt-in would short-circuit at step 2 by returning false when nothing positively declares an access token. It also relies on assertOidcPolicy already being the single boot-time gate for oidc config, which is where a new key's validation belongs.
remediationCheck.newlyRejects: With require_typed_access_token off (the default), nothing changes. With it on, every token that stamps no typ at all is refused — including legitimate access tokens from IdPs that stamp nothing, which is why it must be opt-in and not the default. The doc half rejects nothing.
remediationCheck.testsThatWouldFail: none by default. Turning the flag on would break oidc-token-kinds.test.ts rows 'no typ at all carrying neither nonce nor at_hash' (expects accept) and every row of 'OidcTokenVerifier — signing-algorithm policy', whose mint() sets no typ — which is why the flag must default off and those rows must stay in the default-off partition of the new ISSUER_STYLE axis.
remediationCheck.hidesOrFixes: If only the doc half lands, the code still accepts an ID token from a typ-less IdP whenever the audience collides; the doc turns a silent trap into a documented one, which for a self-hosted single-tenant bridge is most of the value. If only the flag lands and nobody turns it on, nothing changes at all — the default cannot be flipped without breaking legitimate typ-less IdPs, so the doc is the load-bearing half and I am not claiming otherwise.

summary: createRemoteAuthApp returns RemoteAuthServer = OAuthRemoteServer | OidcRemoteServer, and the two halves have opposite close()/listen() contracts: builtin close() is terminal and a later listen() throws, oidc close() is idempotent and re-listenable. Which one a caller gets is decided by cfg.auth.mode, and nothing in the returned type says so.
failure: const s = await createRemoteAuthApp(plugin, cfg, { publicUrl }); await s.listen(p); await s.close(); await s.listen(p2). With cfg.auth.mode 'oidc' this resolves and serves. With cfg.auth.mode 'builtin' it rejects with 'this remote auth app has been closed and cannot listen again'. Same call site, same static type, opposite outcome chosen by a YAML key. packages/bridge-core/src/auth/teardown.test.ts:60 encodes the divergence as expected via its `afterClose: 'terminal' | 're-listenable'` field, so the suite pins the astonishment rather than removing it.
remediation: Make both front doors terminal. Give OidcRemoteServer the same `closed` guard remote.ts:141-150 already has, so that close() -> listen() throws in both modes, and state the contract once on RemoteAuthServer instead of on OAuthRemoteServer alone. A restart-after-close is not a use case either mode serves, and the OIDC door's close() already drops the transport's own state.
testUpgrade: The class is 'a discriminated-union return whose members differ in a runtime contract the type does not discriminate'. Replace teardown.test.ts's per-factory `afterClose` field with a single invariant driven over FACTORIES: every remote-auth factory's close() is terminal, i.e. a second listen() rejects and arms no new interval. A new factory then inherits the assertion instead of being asked to declare which contract it picked — the `afterClose` field is exactly the ratchet that lets a divergence be recorded as intentional. Add a row for any future third mode automatically by deriving FACTORIES from the exported create*App surface, as testing/front-doors.ts already does for DoorName.

remediationCheck.reliesOn: remote.ts's existing pattern: a `let closed = false` captured by the Object.assign'd listen/close pair, wrapping `remote.listen.bind(remote)`. oidc-remote.ts already does `Object.assign(remote, {...})`, so the same three lines drop in without restructuring.

summary: 'The consent page leads with the redirect target because it is the one thing on the page the client cannot choose freely' — an anonymous DCR client chooses its own redirect_uris freely. The real property, which is what the design depends on, is that it cannot LIE about them: the code really does go where the page says.
failure: POST /register with {"redirect_uris":["https://claude.ai.attacker.example/cb"],"client_name":"Claude"} succeeds (201 — I confirmed DCR accepts arbitrary https redirect_uris; only the SDK's SafeUrlSchema blocks javascript:/data:). The consent page then leads with https://claude.ai.attacker.example, a string the client picked. A maintainer reading the comment concludes the leading line is server-controlled and may safely relax the escaping or the demotion of client_name; it is not.
remediation: Restate the invariant as the one that holds, in both places it appears — consent-page.ts:39-43 and the REDIRECT_CORPUS preamble at packages/bridge-core/src/auth/remote.test.ts:825: 'The consent page leads with the redirect target because it is the one thing on the page the client cannot LIE about — the code really is sent there. The client picks it at registration, so it is still attacker-controlled text and is escaped like everything else.'
testUpgrade: The class is 'a comment asserting a provenance (server-controlled vs client-controlled) that the escaping strategy is read against'. Rather than a new test, extend the existing INTERPOLATION_SITES table in oauth-provider.test.ts with a `provenance: 'client-supplied' | 'server-minted'` column and assert that every client-supplied site survives every HOSTILE_PAYLOAD — the redirect target is already a site there, so the column makes its provenance a graded fact next to the assertion instead of a claim in prose. A future site added with provenance 'server-minted' then has to justify itself against the table rather than against a paragraph.

remediationCheck.reliesOn: Nothing in the code path changes; the SDK's SafeUrlSchema at shared/auth.js:147 is what bounds which schemes reach the page, and the escaping in renderConsentPage is what bounds the rest.
remediationCheck.newlyRejects: none
remediationCheck.testsThatWouldFail: none — comment-only edit plus an optional table column. I checked hygiene.test.ts's BANNED_COMMENT_SHAPES: the replacement wording contains none of the six banned phrasings (no ticket ref, no 'Residual:', no 'Latent', no 'We deliberately', no leading 'Note:', no TODO/FIXME/XXX/HACK).
remediationCheck.hidesOrFixes: Nothing is broken in the code — the page is escaped and the demotion of client_name is correct. What stays broken if the comment is left alone is a future reader's model of who controls that line, which is the input to any decision to relax the escaping there.

summary: Six byte-identical copies of `function freePort(): Promise<number>` live in src/auth (remote, oidc-remote, invariants, teardown, error-surface, keycloak.e2e), a seventh sits unexported in src/testing/front-doors.ts, and two more in examples/self-host-remote/test. The shared testing module that already owns fake-plugin, fake-oidc, front-doors and tool-cases already has the helper; it is just not exported.
failure: Not a runtime failure — a review-cost failure. `grep -rln 'function freePort' packages examples` returns 9 files, 6 of them under src/auth. Every one opens a socket on port 0, reads AddressInfo, closes and resolves the port, with an identical TOCTOU window; a fix to that window (e.g. holding the socket until listen) has to be applied nine times or it is applied inconsistently, and a reviewer reading any one auth test file cannot tell whether this copy is the same as the others without diffing all six.
remediation: Export `freePort` from packages/bridge-core/src/testing (the module that already holds front-doors.ts's private copy), and replace the six definitions under src/auth with an import. Leave the examples/ copies alone or point them at the same export, since src/testing is compiled into the tarball and already re-exported through the barrel for fake-oidc.
testUpgrade: The class is 'a test fixture restated per file in a package that already ships a shared testing module'. Add a hygiene row alongside the existing auth-comment and skip-gate rules in packages/bridge-core/src/auth/hygiene.test.ts: scan every *.test.ts under src/** for a top-level `function <name>(` or `const <name> = ` whose body text is byte-identical (after whitespace normalisation) to a definition in another test file, and fail naming the duplicate pair. Driven off a glob rather than a list of known helper names, so the next helper to be copy-pasted — a `pkce()`, a `form()`, a `json()` — is caught the day it lands rather than after the sixth copy.

remediationCheck.reliesOn: src/testing being already compiled into dist (tsconfig excludes only src/**/*.test.ts) and already imported by auth tests — teardown.test.ts imports startFakeOidc from '../testing/fake-oidc.js' and error-surface.test.ts imports from '../testing/front-doors.js', so the import direction is established.
remediationCheck.newlyRejects: none at runtime. The proposed hygiene rule would newly reject any future byte-identical helper pair across test files; I checked the current tree for other exact duplicates and freePort is the one that recurs six times, so the rule fires on exactly the thing it names and would need the six deletions landed first or it starts red.
remediationCheck.testsThatWouldFail: none from the extraction itself — the six bodies are byte-identical, so substituting one import changes no behaviour. The new hygiene rule WOULD fail on the current tree until the extraction lands; that ordering is the point (it must be watched failing against the duplication it is written about).
remediationCheck.hidesOrFixes: Nothing is functionally broken; six identical helpers behave identically today. What stays broken if this is skipped is that the auth directory's 1338- and 1630-line test files each carry their own boilerplate preamble, which is the cost that makes a human reviewer stop reading before the tail of the file — the decay this review's own staging exists to counter.
